# Algorithms Deep Dive — Sorting, Searching, Recursion, Graphs, DP, Greedy, Strings & Math

> **Format:** samjhaane ke liye **Hinglish (roman script)**, aur jo aap interviewer ke
> saamne **bolenge** wo **English** mein — `> **Interview answer:**` blockquotes mein.
> Saara code **Python** mein hai.
>
> Ye document un logon ke liye likha gaya hai jinke paas **formal CS/DSA background
> nahi hai**. QA/SDET ho, Playwright + pytest likhte ho, aur ab senior QA / SDET /
> software engineering interviews ke liye algorithms seriously seekhne hain.

---

## How to Use This Document

Video dekh kar algorithm samajh mein aa jata hai — aur video khatam hote hi udd jata hai.
Wajah simple hai: video mein aapko **result dikhaya** jata hai, **derive** nahi karwaya jata.
Aap dekhte ho ki merge sort O(n log n) hai, par aapne khud kabhi ginn kar nahi nikala ki
`log n` levels kyun bante hain.

Isliye is document mein **har algorithm ke saath ye 10 cheezein hamesha aayengi**, isi order mein:

| # | Section | Isme kya milega |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Kya hai** | Ek plain sentence mein idea + ek real-world analogy, code se **pehle** |
| 2 | **Kyu hai** | Pichhle algorithm mein kya kharabi thi jiski wajah se ye banana pada |
| 3 | **Kaise kaam karta hai** | Mechanism, ASCII diagram ke saath |
| 4 | **Poora dry run** | Chhote input par step-by-step trace, **table** mein, har pass ke baad ki state |
| 5 | **Code** | Python, aur neeche **har line ka numbered explanation** |
| 6 | **Complexity derive karke** | Best / average / worst time, space + recursion stack — **ginn kar**, maan kar nahi |
| 7 | **Stability, in-place, adaptive** | Teenon ka matlab aur kisi ko farak kyun padta hai |
| 8 | **Kab use karna hai / kab nahi** | Practical situations |
| 9 | **Kitne tareeke se optimize** | Har known improvement aur wo kya deta hai, kya leta hai |
| 10 | **Interview answer** | English mein, bolne wala jawab + cross-questions |

### Padhne ka sahi tareeka

1. **Dry run ko skip mat karna.** Wahi asli seekhne wala hissa hai. Ho sake to paper par
   khud saath saath trace karo — table ko haath se bharo.
2. **Code pehle padho, phir line-by-line explanation.** Jo line samajh na aaye, uska number
   dhoondh kar neeche padho.
3. **Complexity derivation ko rat-ta mat maaro.** Ek baar summation ya recursion tree khud
   bana lo, phir wo kabhi nahi bhoolega.
4. **Interview answer ko zor se bolo.** Likh kar samajhna aur bol kar samjhana do alag skills
   hain, aur interview mein doosri wali test hoti hai.

### Notation jo baar baar aayega

| Symbol | Matlab |
|---|---|
| `n` | Input ka size — array mein elements, graph mein vertices, string mein characters |
| `V`, `E` | Graph ke vertices aur edges ki sankhya |
| `O(f(n))` | Upper bound — "isse zyada bura nahi hoga" |
| `Omega(f(n))` | Lower bound — "isse behtar ho hi nahi sakta" |
| `Theta(f(n))` | Upper aur lower dono — "exactly itna hi" |
| `log n` | Base 2 ka log, jab tak alag se na likha ho |
| **Amortised** | Ek operation kabhi kabhi mehnga, par lambe chalte average sasta |

## Part 1: Sorting Algorithms

Sorting sabse purana aur sabse zyada padha jaane wala topic hai, aur iski wajah sirf ye nahi
hai ki data ko order mein lagana zaroori hota hai. Asli wajah ye hai ki **sorting ke andar
poori algorithm design ki alphabet chhupi hui hai**: comparison, swapping, invariants,
divide and conquer, recursion, partitioning, heaps, counting, radix — sab kuch. Agar aapne
das sorting algorithms ko sach mein derive kar liya, to graph aur DP aadhe se zyada aasan ho
jaate hain, kyunki wahan bhi wahi mental tools lagte hain.

---

### Sorting Fundamentals

#### Kya hai

**Sorting matlab** ek collection ke elements ko kisi defined order (chhote se bade, ya bade se
chhote, ya kisi custom rule) mein rearrange karna.

**Real-world analogy:** Aapke haath mein taash ke 13 patte hain. Aap unhe kis tarah lagate ho?
Zyadatar log ek-ek patta uthate hain aur pehle se lage hue patton ke beech uski sahi jagah
par ghusa dete hain. Wo **insertion sort** hai — aapne wo bina padhe hi khud invent kar liya
tha. Doosra insaan poore haath mein se sabse chhota patta dhoondh kar bahar nikaalta hai,
phir bacche hue mein se sabse chhota — wo **selection sort** hai. Teesra insaan patton ko do
dher mein baant kar dono dher alag alag lagata hai aur phir dono ko merge karta hai — wo
**merge sort** hai. Yaani teenon algorithms insaan ke natural behaviours hain; hum sirf unhe
formalise aur measure kar rahe hain.

#### Kyu hai — sorting ka fayda kya hai

Sorting apne aap mein manzil nahi hai, ye **doosri cheezon ko sasta banane ka tareeka** hai:

| Sorted hone ke baad kya sasta ho jata hai | Unsorted cost | Sorted cost |
|---|---|---|
| Kisi element ko dhoondhna | O(n) linear scan | O(log n) binary search |
| Duplicates dhoondhna | O(n²) ya hash set (O(n) space) | O(n) — bas padosi compare karo |
| Median / k-th smallest | O(n) quickselect ya O(n log n) | O(1) — index par jaao |
| Do sorted lists ka intersection | O(n·m) | O(n + m) two pointers |
| Range query "50 se 80 ke beech kitne" | O(n) | O(log n) do binary searches |
| Closest pair (1D) | O(n²) | O(n) — sirf padosi check karo |

QA context mein soch lo: aapke paas 2 lakh test results hain aur aapko har 5 second mein
poochna hai "is duration se dheeme kitne tests the?". Unsorted par har baar 2 lakh scan.
Ek baar sort kar lo (O(n log n)), phir har query O(log n). Ek baar ka kharcha, hamesha ka fayda.

#### Teen properties jo har sort ko define karti hain

Ye teen shabd har sorting interview mein aayenge. Inhe abhi acche se samajh lo, phir har
algorithm ke saath sirf apply karna hoga.

**1. Stability (sthirta)**

Ek sort **stable** hai agar **equal elements ka aapsi order** input se output tak wahi rahe.

```
Input  (name, marks), marks se sort karna hai:
  ("Amit", 90), ("Riya", 85), ("Karan", 90), ("Sana", 85)

Stable sort ka output:
  ("Riya", 85), ("Sana", 85), ("Amit", 90), ("Karan", 90)
   ^^^^^^ Riya Sana se pehle thi -> ab bhi pehle hai
                                     ^^^^^ Amit Karan se pehle tha -> ab bhi pehle hai

Unstable sort ka valid output (bhi sahi hai, par order badal gaya):
  ("Sana", 85), ("Riya", 85), ("Karan", 90), ("Amit", 90)
```

**Isse farak kyun padta hai?** Kyunki stability se aap **multi-key sorting** kar sakte ho
bina complicated comparator likhe. Agar aapko "pehle department se, phir department ke andar
salary se" sort karna hai, to stable sort ke saath aap ulta karo: pehle salary se sort karo,
phir department se sort karo. Department wala sort salary ka order todega nahi (kyunki stable
hai), to result perfect aa jayega. Unstable sort se ye trick kaam nahi karti.

**2. In-place (jagah par)**

Ek sort **in-place** hai agar wo input array ke alawa sirf **O(1) ya O(log n)** extra memory
use kare. Merge sort ko har merge ke liye poora doosra array chahiye — O(n) extra — isliye
wo in-place nahi hai. Quick sort sirf recursion stack use karta hai — O(log n) — isliye use
"in-place" maana jata hai.

**Isse farak kyun padta hai?** Embedded systems, bade datasets, ya jab memory hi bottleneck
ho. 10 GB array ko sort karna hai aur RAM 12 GB hai — merge sort ka O(n) extra aapko maar
dega, quick sort bach jayega.

**3. Adaptive (haalat dekh kar tez)**

Ek sort **adaptive** hai agar input jitna zyada pehle se sorted ho, wo utna hi tez chale.
Insertion sort nearly-sorted data par O(n) ho jata hai. Standard merge sort har haal mein
wahi O(n log n) karta hai, chahe input already sorted ho.

**Isse farak kyun padta hai?** Real world ka data kabhi random nahi hota. Log files time ke
hisaab se almost sorted hote hain, database mein naya record append hota hai, test results
execution order mein aate hain. Adaptive sorts real data par nateeje se kahin behtar chalte hain.
Isi wajah se Python ka Timsort adaptive hai.

#### Comparison sorts ki theoretical limit

Ye ek aisi baat hai jo interview mein bolne par turant senior lagta hai.

Agar aapka algorithm sirf **comparisons** (`a < b`) ke through decide karta hai, to wo
**O(n log n) se tez nahi ho sakta**. Proof ka idea:

```
n elements ke n! possible orderings hain (permutations).
Har comparison ka answer sirf 2 ho sakta hai: yes ya no.
Yaani har comparison decision tree mein ek binary branch hai.

Ek binary tree jiski depth d hai, usme zyada se zyada 2^d leaves hote hain.
Hume n! alag leaves chahiye (har possible ordering ke liye ek).

  2^d  >=  n!
  d    >=  log2(n!)

Stirling se: log2(n!) ~ n·log2(n) - 1.44n
  => d = Omega(n log n)
```

Iska matlab: **koi bhi** comparison-based sort — chahe kitna bhi clever ho — worst case mein
kam se kam ~n log n comparisons karega. Merge sort aur heap sort is limit ko chhoo lete hain,
isliye wo "optimal" comparison sorts hain.

Aur isi se ye bhi samajh aata hai ki counting sort / radix sort O(n) kaise ho jate hain: wo
comparisons karte hi nahi. Wo elements ki **value** ko directly index ki tarah use karte hain,
isliye ye lower bound un par lagta hi nahi.

> **Interview answer:** Sorting is rarely the goal in itself — it's an enabling step. Once data
> is sorted, searching drops from O(n) to O(log n), duplicate detection becomes a single linear
> pass, and range queries become two binary searches. So we pay O(n log n) once to make many
> later operations cheap.
>
> I evaluate any sort on three axes. Stability — do equal elements keep their relative order?
> That matters because with a stable sort you can do multi-key sorting by sorting on the
> secondary key first and the primary key second. In-place — does it use only O(1) or O(log n)
> extra memory? That matters when the dataset approaches available RAM. Adaptive — does it get
> faster on partially sorted input? Real-world data is almost never random, so adaptivity often
> dominates the theoretical numbers.
>
> One important theoretical point: any comparison-based sort has a lower bound of Omega(n log n)
> in the worst case. The argument is a decision tree — each comparison is a binary decision, you
> need n! distinct leaves for the n! possible orderings, so the tree depth is at least log2(n!),
> which is Theta(n log n). Counting sort and radix sort beat that only because they don't compare
> elements at all; they use the values themselves as array indices, so the bound doesn't apply.

> **Cross-question:** *"If stability is so useful, why not always use a stable sort?"*
>
> Because stability usually costs memory. Merge sort is stable but needs O(n) auxiliary space.
> Quicksort and heapsort are in-place but unstable. There are in-place stable sorts — block sort,
> for example — but their constant factors are bad enough that they're rarely worth it. In
> practice you pick stable when you need multi-key ordering or when the elements carry identity
> (records, objects), and in-place when memory is the binding constraint.

> **Cross-question:** *"Is Python's sorted() stable?"*
>
> Yes. Both `list.sort()` and `sorted()` use Timsort, which is guaranteed stable, and CPython
> documents that guarantee — so it's safe to rely on it. That's why the idiom
> `sorted(records, key=lambda r: r.dept)` after `sorted(records, key=lambda r: r.salary)`
> gives you dept-then-salary ordering.

---

### Bubble Sort

#### Kya hai

Bubble sort baar baar array par ghoomta hai aur **har do padosi elements ko compare karke,
agar galat order mein hain to swap kar deta hai**. Har full pass ke baad sabse bada bacha
hua element apni final jagah (array ke end ki taraf) pahunch jata hai — jaise paani mein
hawa ka bubble upar aa jata hai. Isi se naam pada.

**Real-world analogy:** School assembly mein bachche height ke hisaab se line mein lagne
hain. Teacher line ke ek sire se chalti hai aur sirf **do-do bachchon ko compare** karti hai:
"tum lamba ho, tum peeche jao" — swap. Aage badho, agla jodi. Ek poore chakkar ke baad sabse
lamba bachcha line ke end mein pahunch chuka hoga, chahe wo shuru mein kahin bhi khada tha.
Ab teacher dobara shuru se chalti hai, par ab last wale ko chhod deti hai kyunki wo settle
ho chuka hai.

#### Kyu hai

Bubble sort ka "kyu" thoda alag hai — ye kisi problem ko solve karne ke liye nahi bana, ye
**sabse pehla, sabse naive idea** hai jo kisi ko bhi soojhega. Iski value ye hai ki:

1. Ye **correctness ka sabse aasan proof** deta hai. Agar koi bhi padosi jodi galat order
   mein nahi hai, to poora array sorted hai. Bas.
2. Ye **baaki sab algorithms ke liye baseline** hai. Jab hum kehte hain "selection sort
   bubble se behtar hai kyunki kam swaps karta hai", to hume bubble ka number pata hona chahiye.
3. Interview mein iska **early-exit optimisation** poochha jata hai, jo "adaptive" concept
   ko introduce karta hai.

Bubble ki kharabi: ye **bahut zyada swaps** karta hai. Ek element ko apni jagah pahunchne
ke liye ek-ek step karke chalna padta hai. Agar sabse chhota element array ke end par hai,
use shuru tak aane mein n-1 alag alag swaps lagenge, ek pass mein sirf ek kadam. Isi kharabi
ko theek karne ke liye **selection sort** aur **insertion sort** aate hain.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

```
Array: [5, 1, 4, 2, 8]

Pass 1 — poore array par chalo, padosi compare karo:

  [5, 1, 4, 2, 8]      5 > 1 ? haan -> swap
   ^  ^
  [1, 5, 4, 2, 8]      5 > 4 ? haan -> swap
      ^  ^
  [1, 4, 5, 2, 8]      5 > 2 ? haan -> swap
         ^  ^
  [1, 4, 2, 5, 8]      5 > 8 ? nahi -> rehne do
            ^  ^
  [1, 4, 2, 5, 8]      <- pass 1 khatam. 8 apni final jagah par LOCK ho gaya.
                |
                +-- sorted zone (size 1)

Pass 2 — ab sirf pehle 4 elements dekho (8 ko chhod do):

  [1, 4, 2, 5 | 8]     1 > 4 ? nahi
  [1, 4, 2, 5 | 8]     4 > 2 ? haan -> swap
  [1, 2, 4, 5 | 8]     4 > 5 ? nahi
  [1, 2, 4 | 5, 8]     <- 5 lock. sorted zone size 2.

Pass 3 — pehle 3 elements:
  [1, 2, 4 | 5, 8]     1>2 nahi, 2>4 nahi
  [1, 2 | 4, 5, 8]     <- 4 lock.

Pass 4 — pehle 2:
  [1, 2 | 4, 5, 8]     1>2 nahi
  [1 | 2, 4, 5, 8]     <- 2 lock. Bacha hua ek element apne aap sorted hai.
```

**Invariant (wo sach jo har pass ke baad hamesha true rehta hai):** `i` passes ke baad,
array ke **last `i` elements** apni final sorted position par hain aur unse chhote sab elements
unke left mein hain. Ye invariant hi correctness ka proof hai — n-1 passes ke baad last n-1
elements sahi jagah par hain, aur bacha hua pehla element automatically sahi jagah par hai.

#### Poora dry run

Input: `[5, 1, 4, 2, 8]`, n = 5.

**Pass 1** (`i = 0`, inner loop `j` 0 se 3 tak):

| Step | j | Compare | arr[j] > arr[j+1]? | Swap? | Array ke baad |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 5 vs 1 | 5 > 1 → haan | Yes | `[1, 5, 4, 2, 8]` |
| 2 | 1 | 5 vs 4 | 5 > 4 → haan | Yes | `[1, 4, 5, 2, 8]` |
| 3 | 2 | 5 vs 2 | 5 > 2 → haan | Yes | `[1, 4, 2, 5, 8]` |
| 4 | 3 | 5 vs 8 | 5 > 8 → nahi | No | `[1, 4, 2, 5, 8]` |

Pass 1 ke baad: `[1, 4, 2, 5, | 8]` — 4 comparisons, 3 swaps. `8` locked.

**Pass 2** (`i = 1`, inner loop `j` 0 se 2 tak):

| Step | j | Compare | Bada? | Swap? | Array ke baad |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 vs 4 | nahi | No | `[1, 4, 2, 5, 8]` |
| 2 | 1 | 4 vs 2 | haan | Yes | `[1, 2, 4, 5, 8]` |
| 3 | 2 | 4 vs 5 | nahi | No | `[1, 2, 4, 5, 8]` |

Pass 2 ke baad: `[1, 2, 4, | 5, 8]` — 3 comparisons, 1 swap. `5` locked.

**Pass 3** (`i = 2`, `j` 0 se 1 tak):

| Step | j | Compare | Bada? | Swap? | Array ke baad |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 vs 2 | nahi | No | `[1, 2, 4, 5, 8]` |
| 2 | 1 | 2 vs 4 | nahi | No | `[1, 2, 4, 5, 8]` |

Pass 3 ke baad: `[1, 2, | 4, 5, 8]` — 2 comparisons, 0 swaps. `4` locked.

**Pass 4** (`i = 3`, `j` sirf 0):

| Step | j | Compare | Bada? | Swap? | Array ke baad |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 vs 2 | nahi | No | `[1, 2, 4, 5, 8]` |

Pass 4 ke baad: `[1, | 2, 4, 5, 8]` — 1 comparison, 0 swaps. Loop khatam.

**Total:** 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = **10 comparisons**, **4 swaps**. Dhyaan do: pass 3 aur pass 4 mein
ek bhi swap nahi hua — array to pass 2 ke baad hi sorted ho gaya tha, par plain bubble sort
ko ye pata nahi chala aur usne 3 fizool comparisons kar diye. **Yahi wo kharabi hai jise
optimised bubble sort theek karta hai.**

#### Code

```python
def bubble_sort(arr):
    """Array ko chhote se bade order mein sort karta hai. In-place: original list badalti hai."""
    n = len(arr)                                  # 1
    for i in range(n - 1):                        # 2
        for j in range(n - 1 - i):                # 3
            if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]:               # 4
                arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]   # 5
    return arr                                    # 6
```

**Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:**

1. `n = len(arr)` — length ko ek baar variable mein rakh liya. `len()` Python mein O(1) hai
   (list apni length store karti hai), to speed ka fayda mamooli hai, par **readability** ka
   fayda bada hai: neeche do jagah `n` use ho raha hai aur ek jagah badalni ho to ek hi jagah
   badlegi. Agar aap yahan `len(arr)` inline likhte, to code chalta to sahi, bas har iteration
   par ek function call extra hoti.

2. `for i in range(n - 1)` — ye **outer loop**, yaani "kitne passes karne hain". `n - 1` kyun,
   `n` kyun nahi? Kyunki har pass ek element ko lock karta hai. `n - 1` elements lock karne ke
   baad, aakhri bacha hua element automatically apni jagah par hai — usse compare karne ko koi
   bacha hi nahi. Agar aap `range(n)` likh dete to code galat nahi hota, bas ek poora fizool
   pass extra chalta jisme inner loop `range(n-1-(n-1)) = range(0)` hota, yaani kuchh karta hi
   nahi. Yaani `range(n)` likhna = ek wasted iteration.

3. `for j in range(n - 1 - i)` — ye **inner loop**, yaani "is pass mein kitni jodiyaan compare
   karni hain". Do cheezein ho rahi hain:
   - `n - 1` isliye ki `j` aur `j+1` dono valid index hone chahiye. Agar `j` ki max value
     `n-1` hoti, to `arr[j+1]` = `arr[n]` — **IndexError**. Ye sabse common bug hai jo log
     bubble sort likhte waqt karte hain.
   - `- i` isliye ki pichhle `i` passes ne last `i` elements pehle hi lock kar diye hain, unhe
     dobara compare karna waste hai. Agar aap `- i` hata dete to code phir bhi **sahi answer**
     deta (kyunki lock kiye hue elements already sorted hain, unme swap hoga hi nahi), bas
     comparisons n² ke poore ho jaate n²/2 ke bajaye — yaani **2x dheema**.

4. `if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]` — ye **poora algorithm** yahin hai. Strictly greater (`>`) use
   kiya hai, `>=` nahi. Ye choice **stability decide karti hai**: agar do elements barabar
   hain to `>` false dega, swap nahi hoga, unka aapsi order bana rahega — **stable**. Agar
   aap `>=` likh dete to barabar elements bhi swap ho jaate aur sort **unstable** ho jata,
   bina kisi fayde ke — bas extra swaps. Ye ek-character ka farak interview mein pooch liya
   jata hai.

5. `arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]` — Python ka tuple swap. Right side pehle poori
   evaluate hoti hai (ek temporary tuple `(arr[j+1], arr[j])` banti hai), phir left side ko
   assign hoti hai. Isliye temp variable ki zaroorat nahi. Agar aap C-style likhte —
   `arr[j] = arr[j+1]` phir `arr[j+1] = arr[j]` — to **dono jagah same value aa jati** aur
   ek element gum ho jata. Isliye ya to tuple swap karo ya `tmp` variable use karo.

6. `return arr` — Python convention ke hisaab se in-place functions `None` return karte hain
   (jaise `list.sort()`), par yahan `arr` return karna chaining aur testing ke liye
   convenient hai. Yaad rahe: **ye copy nahi return kar raha**, wahi original list return kar
   raha hai jo modify ho chuki hai. Agar caller ko original chahiye tha, to use pehle
   `bubble_sort(arr[:])` bhejna chahiye tha.

#### Complexity derive karke

**Comparisons ginte hain.** Inner loop pass `i` mein exactly `n - 1 - i` baar chalta hai:

```
i = 0  ->  n-1 comparisons
i = 1  ->  n-2 comparisons
i = 2  ->  n-3 comparisons
...
i = n-2 -> 1 comparison

Total = (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 2 + 1
```

Ye ek arithmetic series hai. Iska formula derive karne ka Gauss wala trick:

```
S      =  1  +  2  + ... + (n-2) + (n-1)
S      = (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 2 + 1      (ulta likha)
-----------------------------------------  jodo
2S     =  n  +  n  + ... +  n  +  n        (n-1 baar)
2S     = n(n-1)
S      = n(n-1)/2
```

`n(n-1)/2 = (n² - n)/2`. Bade `n` ke liye `n²` dominate karta hai, constant `1/2` aur `-n/2`
ignore ho jaate hain → **O(n²) comparisons, hamesha**. Chahe array already sorted ho, plain
bubble sort ye saare comparisons karega hi.

**Swaps ginte hain.**
- **Best case** (already sorted): 0 swaps. Comparisons phir bhi n(n-1)/2.
- **Worst case** (reverse sorted): har comparison par swap → n(n-1)/2 swaps → **O(n²)**.
- **Average case**: har jodi ke inverted hone ka chance 50% → ~n(n-1)/4 swaps → phir bhi O(n²).

**Ek aur tareeka soch ka — inversions.** Ek "inversion" matlab aisi jodi `(i, j)` jahan
`i < j` par `arr[i] > arr[j]`. Bubble sort ka har swap **exactly ek inversion hataata hai**
(kyunki wo padosi swap karta hai). Reverse-sorted array mein n(n-1)/2 inversions hote hain,
isliye utne hi swaps lagenge. Ye insight aage insertion sort ke complexity mein bhi kaam aayegi.

**Space:** Sirf `i`, `j`, `n` — teen variables, input size se independent → **O(1) auxiliary
space**. Koi recursion nahi, to stack bhi O(1).

| Case | Time | Kab hota hai |
|---|---|---|
| Best | O(n²) — plain version | Already sorted (par plain version detect nahi karta) |
| Average | O(n²) | Random order |
| Worst | O(n²) | Reverse sorted |
| Space | O(1) | Hamesha |

#### Stability, in-place, adaptive

| Property | Bubble sort | Kyun |
|---|---|---|
| **Stable** | Haan | `>` use hota hai, `>=` nahi — barabar elements kabhi swap nahi hote, to unka original order intact rehta hai |
| **In-place** | Haan | Sirf constant extra variables, koi extra array nahi |
| **Adaptive** | **Nahi** (plain version) | Sorted input par bhi poore n(n-1)/2 comparisons karta hai. Early-exit version isse adaptive bana deta hai |

**Kisko farak padta hai?** Stability ka fayda tab hai jab aap objects sort kar rahe ho —
jaise test results ko `duration` se sort karo par same duration wale tests apne execution
order mein hi rahen. In-place ka fayda tab hai jab memory tight ho. Adaptive na hona bubble
sort ki sabse badi practical kami hai, aur wahi agle section mein theek hogi.

#### Kab use karna hai / kab nahi

**Use karo jab:**
- Aapko **padhaana** hai ya khud seekhna hai — sabse aasan mental model.
- Array bahut chhota hai (n < 10) aur code simplicity sab se zyada matter karti hai.
- Aapko sirf ye check karna hai ki array sorted hai ya nahi (ek single pass, no swaps → sorted).

**Mat use karo jab:**
- Production code mein — kabhi bhi. `sorted()` har haal mein behtar hai.
- n > ~50 — insertion sort same O(n²) hote hue bhi practically 2-3x tez hai kyunki wo swaps
  ki jagah shifts karta hai aur nearly-sorted data par O(n) ho jata hai.
- Interview coding round mein solution ke taur par — interviewer ise "didn't think about it"
  ka signal maanta hai. Haan, agar wo khud bubble sort poochhe to alag baat hai.

#### Kitne tareeke se optimize

| # | Optimisation | Kya deta hai | Kya leta hai |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Early exit** — agar ek poore pass mein koi swap na ho to break | Best case O(n²) → **O(n)**, algorithm adaptive ban jata hai | Ek boolean flag, na ke barabar cost |
| 2 | **Last-swap boundary** — ye yaad rakho ki last swap kis index par hua tha, agle pass mein bas wahin tak jao | Partially sorted tails par kaafi passes bachte hain | Ek extra integer |
| 3 | **Cocktail shaker sort** — ek pass left→right, agla right→left | "Turtles" (chhote elements jo end par hain) tez aage aate hain; roughly 2x kam passes | Code lamba, complexity phir bhi O(n²) |
| 4 | **Comb sort** — shuru mein door ke elements compare karo (gap = n/1.3), gap dheere dheere 1 tak lao | Practically O(n log n) ke aas paas, turtles turant hat jaate hain | Ab ye bubble sort nahi raha, ye shell sort ka cousin hai; stability chali jati hai |
| 5 | **Odd-even transposition sort** — alternate passes mein sirf odd ya even index pairs | Parallel hardware par har pass ke saare comparisons ek saath ho sakte hain | Sequential machine par koi fayda nahi |

Inme se #1 wo hai jo aapko interview mein khud se bolna chahiye, aur wahi hum agle section
mein poora likh rahe hain.

> **Interview answer:** Bubble sort repeatedly walks the array comparing adjacent pairs and
> swapping them when they're out of order. After the first full pass the largest element has
> bubbled to the last position, after the second pass the second largest is in place, and so on
> — so after i passes the last i elements are final. That invariant is the correctness argument.
>
> Complexity: the inner loop runs n-1, then n-2, down to 1 times, and that sum is n(n-1)/2, so
> it's O(n²) comparisons in every case. Swaps are O(n²) in the worst case — reverse-sorted input
> — and zero in the best case. Space is O(1), it's in-place, and it's stable because we swap only
> on a strict greater-than, so equal elements never cross each other.
>
> The plain version is not adaptive: it does the full n(n-1)/2 comparisons even on already-sorted
> input. The standard fix is a swapped flag — if a full pass completes with no swaps the array is
> sorted and we break, which makes the best case O(n). In practice I'd never ship bubble sort;
> insertion sort has the same asymptotic class but much better constants because it shifts rather
> than swaps, and it's genuinely adaptive.

> **Cross-question:** *"Why does one pass of bubble sort guarantee the maximum ends up last?"*
>
> Because once the scan reaches the maximum element, every subsequent comparison has the maximum
> on the left, so every one of those comparisons swaps it one step right. There's nothing that can
> stop it, so it travels unbroken to the end of the pass range.

> **Cross-question:** *"Bubble sort does O(n²) swaps and selection sort does O(n) swaps. Does that
> make selection sort faster?"*
>
> On memory writes, yes — selection sort is the better choice when writes are expensive, like on
> flash storage or EEPROM. But both do O(n²) comparisons, so asymptotically they're the same class,
> and on ordinary RAM the difference is a constant factor. The bigger practical winner is insertion
> sort, which is adaptive: on nearly sorted data it approaches O(n) while both bubble and selection
> stay at O(n²).

---

### Optimised Bubble Sort

#### Kya hai

Wahi bubble sort, par ek chhote se sawaal ke saath: **"is poore pass mein kya maine ek bhi
swap kiya?"** Agar jawab "nahi" hai, to iska matlab koi bhi padosi jodi galat order mein
nahi thi, yaani **array pehle hi sorted hai** — aur hum turant ruk jaate hain.

**Real-world analogy:** Wahi assembly line wali teacher. Ek poora chakkar lagane ke baad
agar usne ek bhi bachche ko idhar-udhar nahi kiya, to line already sahi hai — ab aur chakkar
lagane ka koi matlab nahi. Plain bubble sort wali teacher bewakoofi se poore n-1 chakkar
lagati rehti hai chahe line pehle din se hi sahi ho.

#### Kyu hai

Plain bubble sort ki dry run mein humne dekha tha: `[5,1,4,2,8]` pass 2 ke baad hi sorted ho
gaya tha, par algorithm ne pass 3 aur pass 4 bhi chalaye — 3 fizool comparisons.

Chhote array par ye 3 comparisons ki baat hai. Par socho **10,000 elements** ka array jo
pehle se sorted hai (bahut common — database se sorted data aa raha hai, ya aapne pehle hi
sort kar liya tha aur dobara sort call ho gaya). Plain bubble sort **5 crore comparisons**
karega. Optimised version **9,999 comparisons** karke ruk jayega. Ye 5000x ka farak hai, aur
ye ek boolean variable ki keemat par mila hai.

Yahi is optimisation ka poora point hai: **algorithm ko adaptive banana** — input ki halat
dekh kar kaam kam karna.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

```
Har pass ki shuruaat mein:  swapped = False

  Jab bhi koi swap ho:      swapped = True

Pass ke end mein:
  agar swapped abhi bhi False hai
      -> is poore pass mein koi padosi jodi galat order mein nahi thi
      -> "har i ke liye arr[i] <= arr[i+1]"  == definition of sorted
      -> break
```

Ye kyun **guaranteed** sahi hai? Kyunki "sorted" ki definition hi yahi hai: har padosi jodi
sahi order mein. Bubble sort ka ek poora pass har padosi jodi ko exactly ek baar check karta
hai. Agar sab pass ho gaye, to array sorted hai. Ye koi heuristic ya guess nahi, ye **proof**
hai.

**Doosra optimisation — last swap boundary:**

```
Pass ke dauraan yaad rakho: aakhri swap kis index par hua?  ->  last_swap

Agar last swap index 3 par hua, iska matlab index 4 se aage sab jodiyaan sahi thin
      [ ?  ?  ?  ?  | sorted sorted sorted ]
                  ^
              last_swap

Agle pass mein sirf index 0 se last_swap tak jao. Ek pass mein kai elements ek saath lock ho
sakte hain, sirf ek nahi.
```

Example: `[2, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]`. Pass 1 mein sirf ek swap hoga (index 0 par), baaki sab
comparisons pass ho jayenge. `last_swap = 0`. Ab agle pass ki range `0 se 0` hai — yaani
inner loop chalega hi nahi, swapped False rahega, break. Total: 7 + 0 comparisons. Simple
early-exit version 7 + 7 = 14 karta. Boundary version ne aadhe kaam mein khatam kiya.

#### Poora dry run

Do inputs par trace karte hain taaki dono kaam dikh jaayen.

**Dry run A — input `[5, 1, 4, 2, 8]` (wahi jo plain version mein tha):**

**Pass 1** (`swapped = False` se shuru, range `j` = 0..3):

| j | Compare | Swap? | Array | swapped | last_swap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 5 vs 1 | Yes | `[1,5,4,2,8]` | True | 0 |
| 1 | 5 vs 4 | Yes | `[1,4,5,2,8]` | True | 1 |
| 2 | 5 vs 2 | Yes | `[1,4,2,5,8]` | True | 2 |
| 3 | 5 vs 8 | No | `[1,4,2,5,8]` | True | 2 |

Pass 1 end: `swapped = True` → continue. `last_swap = 2` → agla pass sirf j = 0..1.

**Pass 2** (`swapped = False`, range `j` = 0..1):

| j | Compare | Swap? | Array | swapped | last_swap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 vs 4 | No | `[1,4,2,5,8]` | False | — |
| 1 | 4 vs 2 | Yes | `[1,2,4,5,8]` | True | 1 |

Pass 2 end: `swapped = True` → continue. `last_swap = 1` → agla pass j = 0..0.

**Pass 3** (`swapped = False`, range `j` = 0..0):

| j | Compare | Swap? | Array | swapped |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 vs 2 | No | `[1,2,4,5,8]` | False |

Pass 3 end: `swapped = False` → **BREAK**.

**Comparison:** plain bubble = 10 comparisons. Early-exit + boundary = 4 + 2 + 1 = **7
comparisons**. 30% kam, aur ye chhota input hai.

**Dry run B — input `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` (already sorted):**

**Pass 1** (`swapped = False`, j = 0..3):

| j | Compare | Swap? | swapped |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 vs 2 | No | False |
| 1 | 2 vs 3 | No | False |
| 2 | 3 vs 4 | No | False |
| 3 | 4 vs 5 | No | False |

Pass 1 end: `swapped = False` → **BREAK**.

**Total: 4 comparisons, 0 swaps.** Plain bubble sort ne 10 comparisons kiye hote. n = 10,000
par: 9,999 vs 5,00,00,000. **Yahi adaptive hone ka matlab hai.**

#### Code

```python
def bubble_sort_optimised(arr):
    """Early-exit + last-swap-boundary ke saath bubble sort."""
    n = len(arr)                                  # 1
    end = n - 1                                   # 2
    while end > 0:                                # 3
        last_swap = 0                             # 4
        for j in range(end):                      # 5
            if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]:               # 6
                arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]   # 7
                last_swap = j                     # 8
        end = last_swap                           # 9
    return arr                                    # 10
```

**Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:**

1. `n = len(arr)` — length ek baar nikaal li. Baaki poore function mein array ki length
   badalti nahi, isliye ek baar nikaalna safe hai.

2. `end = n - 1` — `end` ka matlab hai "is pass mein `j` kahan tak jayega (exclusive)".
   Shuruaat mein `n - 1`, kyunki `j` ki max value `n-2` honi chahiye taaki `arr[j+1]` valid
   rahe. Agar aap `end = n` likh dete, to pehle hi pass mein `arr[n]` par **IndexError**.

3. `while end > 0` — `for` ki jagah `while` isliye use kiya kyunki **passes ki sankhya
   pehle se pata nahi hai**. Ye input par depend karti hai — sorted input par 1 pass,
   reverse input par n-1. `for i in range(n-1)` likh kar `break` bhi kar sakte the, par
   `while` zyada honest hai: ye seedha bolta hai "jab tak unsorted region bacha hai, chalte
   raho". Condition `> 0` hai, `>= 0` nahi — agar `end = 0` ho gaya to `range(0)` khali hai,
   loop kuchh nahi karta aur infinite loop ban jata. **Ye classic infinite-loop bug hai.**

4. `last_swap = 0` — **har pass ki shuruaat mein reset**. Ye reset sabse important line hai.
   Agar aap ise `while` ke bahar rakh dete, to pichhle pass ki value carry ho jati aur `end`
   kabhi ghatta nahi — infinite loop. Value `0` isliye rakhi hai kyunki wo "koi swap nahi hua"
   ko bhi represent karti hai: agar pass ke baad `last_swap` abhi bhi 0 hai to `end = 0` ho
   jayega aur `while` khatam. Yaani **ek hi variable early-exit flag aur boundary dono ka
   kaam kar raha hai** — alag `swapped` boolean ki zaroorat hi nahi.

5. `for j in range(end)` — `j` 0 se `end-1` tak. Har iteration mein `arr[j]` aur `arr[j+1]`
   ki jodi. Max `j` = `end - 1`, to max index touch hoga `end` — jo hamesha valid hai kyunki
   `end <= n-1`.

6. `if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]` — wahi strict greater-than. Stability ke liye zaroori.

7. Tuple swap — same as before.

8. `last_swap = j` — **`j` store kar rahe hain, `j+1` nahi.** Ye off-by-one sochne layak hai.
   Agar swap index `j` par hua, to `arr[j]` aur `arr[j+1]` dono touch hue. Iska matlab index
   `j+1` ke baad wali jodiyaan pakka sahi thin. Agle pass mein hume `j = 0` se `j = last_swap - 1`
   tak jaana chahiye... par actually hume `j = last_swap` tak bhi jaana chahiye kyunki `arr[j]`
   ki value badal gayi hai aur uske left wale se dobara compare karna pad sakta hai. Isliye
   `end = last_swap` set karte hain jisse `range(end)` `j` ko `0..last_swap-1` deta hai —
   yaani jodi `(last_swap-1, last_swap)` tak. Ye exactly utna hai jitna zaroori hai. Agar aap
   `last_swap = j + 1` likh dete to ek extra fizool comparison har pass mein hoti (galat nahi,
   bas slightly slow).

9. `end = last_swap` — agle pass ki boundary set. Agar is pass mein koi swap nahi hua to
   `last_swap` abhi bhi 0 hai → `end = 0` → `while` condition fail → **early exit**. Agar
   swap hua to `end` chhota ho gaya → agla pass chhota. Dono optimisations ek line mein.

10. `return arr` — in-place modified array.

**Ek simpler version bhi jaan lo** (agar interview mein sirf early exit poochha jaye):

```python
def bubble_sort_early_exit(arr):
    n = len(arr)                        # 1
    for i in range(n - 1):              # 2
        swapped = False                 # 3
        for j in range(n - 1 - i):      # 4
            if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]:     # 5
                arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]  # 6
                swapped = True          # 7
        if not swapped:                 # 8
            break                       # 9
    return arr                          # 10
```

1. Length nikaali.
2. Outer loop, `n-1` passes maximum.
3. `swapped = False` — **loop ke andar**, har pass ke liye fresh. Bahar rakhne se pehla swap
   hone ke baad ye hamesha True rehta aur early exit kabhi trigger nahi hota — optimisation
   silently mar jati, code phir bhi sahi answer deta. **Aisa bug pakadna mushkil hai** kyunki
   test pass ho jate hain, bas performance nahi milti.
4. Inner loop, `- i` se already-locked tail skip.
5. Strict greater-than compare.
6. Swap.
7. `swapped = True` — flag set. Note: hum sirf `True` set karte hain, kabhi `False` nahi —
   ek bhi swap kaafi hai batane ke liye ki array abhi sorted nahi tha.
8. `if not swapped` — poora pass bina swap ke nikla → sorted.
9. `break` — bahar. `return` bhi likh sakte the, par `break` se function ka single exit point
   bana rehta hai jo debug karne mein aasan hai.
10. Return.

#### Complexity derive karke

**Best case — already sorted input:**

```
Pass 1: n-1 comparisons, 0 swaps
        last_swap = 0  ->  end = 0  ->  while khatam

Total comparisons = n - 1  ->  O(n)
Total swaps       = 0      ->  O(1)
```

**Ye pehla algorithm hai jiska best case O(n) hai.** Isi ko "adaptive" kehte hain.

**Worst case — reverse sorted `[5,4,3,2,1]`:**

Har pass mein har comparison swap banti hai, to `last_swap` hamesha `end - 1` hota hai,
yaani `end` har pass mein sirf 1 ghatta hai — exactly plain bubble sort jaisa:

```
(n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n-1)/2  ->  O(n²)
```

Optimisation ne worst case mein **kuchh nahi bachaya**. Ye important hai: optimisation best
aur average case ko theek karti hai, worst case ki asymptotic class wahi rehti hai.

**Average case:** Random permutation par expected passes ~n, aur har pass O(n) → **O(n²)**.
Constant factor plain version se chhota hai (typically 30-40% kam comparisons), par class wahi.

**Space:** `n`, `end`, `last_swap`, `j` — 4 variables → **O(1)**.

| Case | Comparisons | Swaps | Kab |
|---|---|---|---|
| Best | **O(n)** | 0 | Already sorted |
| Average | O(n²) | O(n²) | Random |
| Worst | O(n²) | O(n²) | Reverse sorted |
| Space | O(1) | — | Hamesha |

**Nearly-sorted ka special case:** Agar array mein sirf `k` inversions hain (k chhota), to
swaps exactly `k` honge (kyunki har swap ek inversion hataata hai) aur passes ~`k` se bandhe
honge. Yaani nearly-sorted par ye practically O(n·k) chalta hai, jo `k` chhota hone par O(n)
ke kareeb hai.

#### Stability, in-place, adaptive

| Property | Value | Kyun |
|---|---|---|
| **Stable** | Haan | `>` strict comparison — equal elements swap nahi hote |
| **In-place** | Haan | O(1) extra memory |
| **Adaptive** | **Haan** | Sorted par O(n), nearly-sorted par inversions ke proportional. Yahi wo cheez hai jo plain version mein nahi thi |

**Adaptive hone ka practical matlab:** QA mein aap aksar aisa data sort karte ho jo pehle se
mostly sorted hai — timestamps, IDs, test execution order. Adaptive algorithm us structure ka
faayda uthata hai. Yahi soch aage **Timsort** tak le jayegi, jo isi idea ko industrial level
par le jata hai.

#### Kab use karna hai / kab nahi

**Use karo jab:**
- Interview mein bubble sort poochha gaya ho — **ye version likho, plain nahi**. Ye dikhata
  hai ki aap best case ke baare mein sochte ho.
- Aapko sirf "kya array sorted hai?" check karna ho — pehla pass hi bata dega.
- Bahut chhota, almost-sorted data aur aap external library nahi use kar sakte.

**Mat use karo jab:**
- Random ya reverse-sorted data — worst case abhi bhi O(n²).
- Production — insertion sort same properties ke saath consistently tez hai.

#### Kitne tareeke se optimize

| # | Optimisation | Kya deta hai | Kya leta hai |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Early exit flag | Best case O(n), adaptive | 1 boolean |
| 2 | Last-swap boundary (upar wala code) | Ek pass mein kai elements lock, ~30-40% kam comparisons average par | 1 integer, flag ki zaroorat khatam |
| 3 | Cocktail shaker (bidirectional) | "Turtle" problem — chhota element jo end par hai — ka fix. Passes ~aadhe | Code double, worst case wahi O(n²) |
| 4 | Comb sort (gap shrink 1.3x) | Practically ~O(n log n), turtles turant fix | Stability chali gayi, ab ye shell sort family hai |
| 5 | Insertion sort par switch kar do | Har case mein behtar | "Ab ye bubble sort nahi raha" |

Point #5 ek asli interview insight hai: **bubble sort ka har optimisation aapko insertion
sort ya shell sort ki taraf le jata hai.** Agar aapko bubble sort optimize karna hi hai, to
sabse acchi optimisation hai use replace kar dena.

> **Interview answer:** The plain bubble sort wastes work: it keeps running passes even after
> the array has become sorted. The standard fix is a swapped flag — if a complete pass performs
> no swaps, then no adjacent pair is out of order, which is exactly the definition of sorted, so
> we can break immediately. That turns the best case from O(n²) into O(n) and makes the algorithm
> adaptive.
>
> A second, better optimisation is to remember the index of the last swap in each pass. Everything
> to the right of that index is already in final position, so the next pass only needs to scan up
> to that boundary. That can lock multiple elements per pass instead of just one, and it subsumes
> the flag — if the last-swap index stays at zero, no swap happened, and the loop terminates
> naturally.
>
> Neither optimisation helps the worst case. On reverse-sorted input every comparison still swaps,
> the boundary shrinks by one each pass, and we're back to n(n-1)/2 comparisons — O(n²). So it
> improves the best and average cases, not the asymptotic worst case.

> **Cross-question:** *"Where would you initialise the swapped flag, and what breaks if you get
> it wrong?"*
>
> Inside the outer loop, at the start of each pass. If you initialise it outside, the first swap
> anywhere sets it True permanently and the early exit never fires. The dangerous part is that the
> code still produces correct output — only the performance benefit silently disappears — so unit
> tests won't catch it. You'd only see it in a benchmark.

> **Cross-question:** *"You store `last_swap = j` rather than `j + 1`. Why?"*
>
> Because after a swap at index j, the value at position j has changed and may still need to move
> further left, so position j must remain inside the next pass's range. Setting `end = last_swap`
> makes `range(end)` cover j from 0 to last_swap - 1, which compares pairs up through
> `(last_swap - 1, last_swap)` — exactly the region that can still contain an inversion. Using
> `j + 1` would be correct too, just one redundant comparison per pass.
