### How to Recognise a DP Problem

Ye section aur agla — is poore Part ke sabse kaam ke do sections hain. Algorithm yaad rakhna
aasan hai; **pehchaanna** ki problem DP hai, mushkil hai.

#### Teen signals jo saath aane chahiye

**1. Optimisation ya counting ka shabd.** "Minimum", "maximum", "longest", "how many ways",
"is it possible". Agar problem **saare** answers maang rahi hai (`"list all partitions"`), to
DP nahi — backtracking. DP ek **number** ya **ek** best answer deta hai.

**2. Choices ka sequence.** Aap answer ko **ek-ek decision** karke bana sakte ho: ye item lo ya
chhodo, yahan cut lagao ya nahi, ye character match karo ya skip. Agar ek hi formula se answer
aa raha hai (jaise `C(n, k)`), DP ki zaroorat nahi.

**3. Overlapping subproblems.** Recursion likho aur dekho ki **wahi arguments** dobara aa rahe
hain ya nahi. Ye sabse zaroori signal hai — **iske bina DP nahi hai, sirf divide and conquer hai.**

Merge sort mein `sort(0,4)` kabhi dobara call nahi hoti — isliye merge sort **DP nahi hai**,
chahe wo optimal substructure rakhta ho. Fibonacci mein `fib(3)` teen baar aati hai — **wahi DP
banata hai.**

#### Practical test — 60 second mein

1. **Brute force recursion likho**, bhale hi exponential ho. Sirf signature aur recurrence.
2. **Arguments ginno.** Kitne alag `(i, j, ...)` combinations possible hain? Agar wo polynomial
   hain aur recursion tree exponential hai, to **repeat ho rahe hain** → DP.
3. `@lru_cache` laga do. Agar kaam kar gaya, DP mil gaya. Bottom-up baad mein.

Ye teesra step interview mein bilkul valid hai — top-down memo likh do, phir bolo "I can convert
this to bottom-up and drop the recursion stack if you want."

#### Kab DP **nahi** hai — worked counterexample

**Problem:** "N cities, har pair ke beech distance, sabse chhota tour jo har city ek baar
visit kare." (TSP)

Ye optimisation hai, choices ka sequence hai, aur subproblems overlap bhi karte hain. **Phir
bhi standard DP fail ho jaata hai** — kyunki state sirf "abhi kis city par hoon" nahi ho sakti;
"kaunsi cities visit ho chuki hain" bhi state ka hissa hai. Aur wo ek **subset** hai, to states
`2ⁿ · n` ho jaate hain. Bitmask DP kaam karta hai par sirf n ≤ 20 tak. **Seekh:** DP tab tak
useful hai jab tak state space polynomial hai — warna wo sirf brute force ka organised version
hai.

**Doosra counterexample:** "Array ko sort karo." Optimisation lagta hai, par yahan **koi
overlapping subproblem nahi** — har subarray alag hai. Ye divide and conquer hai, DP nahi.

#### Greedy vs DP — pehla filter

Agar har step par ek **local** rule se optimal answer nikal aata hai (aur aap wo prove kar sakte
ho), greedy kaafi hai — DP overkill hai. Agar local best baad mein galat sabit ho sakta hai
(coin change `[1,3,4]`, amount 6), to DP chahiye. **Jab shaq ho, DP likho** — wo hamesha sahi
hoga, bas dhima hoga. Greedy tabhi likho jab exchange argument dimaag mein taiyaar ho.

> **Interview answer:** I look for three things together. First, the question asks for a minimum,
> a maximum, a count of ways, or a yes-no feasibility — not for the full list of solutions, which
> would mean backtracking instead. Second, the answer is built through a sequence of choices, so I
> can write a recurrence over "what do I do with the current element". Third, and most importantly,
> that recursion revisits the same arguments — without overlapping subproblems it's divide and
> conquer, not DP. Merge sort has optimal substructure but never repeats a subproblem, which is
> exactly why memoising it buys nothing.
>
> My practical method is to write the brute-force recursion first, count the distinct argument
> combinations, and if that count is polynomial while the recursion tree is exponential, memoise
> it. In an interview I'll write the top-down version with an lru_cache, confirm it's correct, and
> then offer to convert it to bottom-up to remove the recursion stack.
>
> The limit worth naming is when the state has to include a set rather than an index — travelling
> salesman, for example. The DP is correct but the state space is two to the n, so it's only a
> practical answer for small inputs.

---

### How to Define the State

State galat define kar di to baaki sab bekaar hai. Ye sabse zyada slip yahin hoti hai.

#### State kya hoti hai

State = **minimum information** jo aapko chahiye taaki aage ke decisions le sako, **bina ye jaane
ki aap yahan tak pahunche kaise**. Isi ko "Markov property" kehte hain. Agar aage ka answer
past ke kisi detail par depend karta hai jo state mein nahi hai, to state **incomplete** hai.

#### Teen sawaal poochho

**1. Main abhi kahan hoon?** — index, position, remaining capacity. Ye lagbhag hamesha state ka
hissa hota hai.
**2. Aage ka faisla kis cheez par depend karta hai?** — bacha hua budget, pichhla element,
kitne transactions ho chuke. Har aisi cheez ek **dimension** hai.
**3. Kya main state ko chhota kar sakta hoon?** — agar ek dimension ki value sirf 2-3 ho sakti
hai (bought/not bought), to wo boolean flag hai, poora array nahi.

#### Do standard shapes

| Shape | Matlab | Kahan |
|---|---|---|
| `dp[i]` = **`i` tak ka answer** (prefix) | `i` ke baad ki cheezein irrelevant | Coin change, climbing stairs |
| `dp[i]` = **`i` par khatam hone wala** answer | `i` mandatory hai answer mein | LIS, max subarray, house robber ke variants |

Ye do alag cheezein hain aur inko mila dena classic bug hai. **Prefix wale mein answer `dp[n]`
hota hai; "ending at i" wale mein `max(dp)` hota hai.** LIS mein `dp[-1]` return karna isi
confusion se aata hai.

#### Worked example — state galat se sahi tak

**Problem:** stock prices ka array, **do** transactions tak allowed, maximum profit.

**Attempt 1:** `dp[i]` = day `i` tak ka max profit. **Fail** — kyunki aage ka faisla is baat par
depend karta hai ki **kitni transactions bachi hain** aur **abhi stock haath mein hai ya nahi**.
Ye dono information `dp[i]` mein nahi hai.

**Attempt 2:** `dp[i][k]` = day `i` tak, `k` transactions use karke max profit. **Abhi bhi
fail** — "stock haath mein hai ya nahi" missing hai. Agar haath mein hai, to aaj bech sakta hoon;
nahi hai to sirf khareed sakta hoon. Do bilkul alag situations, ek hi state.

**Attempt 3:** `dp[i][k][holding]` jahan `holding ∈ {0, 1}`. **Ab complete hai.** Transitions:
`dp[i][k][0] = max(dp[i-1][k][0], dp[i-1][k][1] + price[i])` (hold karo ya becho),
`dp[i][k][1] = max(dp[i-1][k][1], dp[i-1][k-1][0] - price[i])` (hold karo ya khareedo).

**Seekh:** state tab tak badhao jab tak transition **deterministic** na ban jaaye. Agar transition
likhte waqt aapko "par ye to depend karta hai ki…" bolna pad raha hai, wahi missing dimension hai.

#### State chhoti rakhne ke tareeke

- **Symmetry** — `dp[i][j]` mein agar sirf `j - i` matter karta hai, to ek dimension kaafi hai.
- **Rolling** — agar sirf pichhli row chahiye, `dp[i]` ki jagah do arrays.
- **Bitmask** — subset chahiye aur n chhota hai (≤ 20) to integer mein pack karo.
- **Normalise** — `dp[remaining]` aksar `dp[used]` se chhota hota hai agar capacity bandhi hai.

> **Interview answer:** The state is the smallest amount of information that makes the rest of the
> decisions independent of how I got there. I build it by asking two questions: where am I, and
> what else does the next decision depend on. Each thing in that second answer becomes a dimension.
>
> The test I apply is whether I can write the transition without saying "but that depends on".
> The stock-trading problem is the clearest example — dp[day] is not enough, dp[day][transactions
> used] is still not enough, and only dp[day][transactions][holding] makes the transition
> deterministic, because whether I currently own the stock decides which moves are even legal.
>
> The other distinction I'm careful about is prefix states versus ending-at states. dp[i] meaning
> "best answer using the first i elements" gives the answer at dp[n]; dp[i] meaning "best answer
> that ends at i" gives the answer as the max over the whole array. Longest increasing subsequence
> is the ending-at kind, and returning dp of the last index instead of the maximum is the single
> most common bug in that problem.

---

## Part 6: Greedy Algorithms

Greedy sabse aasan likhne wali cheez hai aur sabse mushkil **prove** karne wali. Code aksar
paanch line ka hota hai. Interview mein sawaal ye nahi hota ki "greedy likh sakte ho" — sawaal
ye hota hai ki **"ye greedy sahi kyun hai?"** Isliye is Part mein do sections code se pehle aate
hain: correctness kaise sabit karte hain, aur exchange argument kya hai.

---

### What Makes Greedy Provably Correct

#### Do conditions — dono chahiye

**1. Greedy choice property.** Ek **globally optimal solution aisa maujood hai** jo pehli greedy
choice ko include karta hai. Dhyaan do: ye nahi kaha ki "greedy choice hamesha optimal solution
mein hoti hai" — kaha ye hai ki **koi ek** optimal solution use include karta hai. Ye farak
chhota lagta hai par proof ka poora dhaancha isi par khada hai.

**2. Optimal substructure.** Pehli choice lene ke baad jo bachta hai, wo **usi problem ka chhota
version** hai, aur uska optimal solution poore ka optimal solution banata hai.

DP mein optimal substructure hota hai par greedy choice property **nahi** hoti — isliye DP saare
options try karta hai. Greedy mein dono hote hain, isliye wo **ek** option try karke aage badh
jaata hai. **Yahi poora farak hai.**

#### Proof ka standard structure

Greedy correctness ke do standard proofs hote hain:

**Exchange argument** (agla section) — optimal solution lo, usse greedy jaisa banao bina kharaab
kiye. Sabse zyada use hota hai.

**Greedy stays ahead** — induction se dikhao ki har step `k` par greedy ka partial solution kisi
bhi doosre solution ke partial solution se **kam se kam utna hi accha** hai. Activity selection
ke liye: greedy ke pehle `k` activities ka finish time har doosre valid choice ke `k`-th finish
time se `<=` hota hai. Agar greedy har jagah aage hai, to wo peeche kaise reh sakta hai.

#### Matroid — jab greedy hamesha kaam karta hai

Formally, greedy **hamesha** optimal hota hai agar problem ek **matroid** hai — do properties:
subsets of a valid set are valid (hereditary), aur agar ek valid set doosre se bada hai to bade
wale se ek element utha kar chhote wale mein daala ja sakta hai (exchange property). **Kruskal's
MST isi wajah se kaam karta hai** — forests ek matroid banate hain. Interview mein ye naam le
dena bohot achha signal hai, par baaki sab problems ke liye exchange argument hi likhna padega.

#### Ek chhota worked proof — fractional knapsack

**Claim:** highest value/weight ratio wala item pehle poora bharna optimal hai.
**Proof:** maano optimal solution `O` mein us item (ratio `r_max`) ka `x` weight hai jabki hum
`y > x` bhar sakte the. To `O` mein kisi doosre item ka `y - x` weight hai jiska ratio `r < r_max`.
Us `y - x` weight ko hata kar highest-ratio item se badal do. Weight same rahega, value
**badhegi ya barabar rahegi** (`(y-x)·r_max >= (y-x)·r`). Matlab `O` se buri nahi, aur ab wo
greedy choice include karti hai. **Isliye greedy choice safe hai.** ∎

#### Red flags — greedy shayad galat hai

- Choices ek doosre ko **constrain** karti hain (0/1 knapsack — ek item lene se capacity kam
  hoti hai jo baad ke better combos rok deti hai).
- Answer mein **combination** matter karti hai, individual elements nahi (coin change).
- Aapko "yahan lena behtar hai ya wahan" ka **trade-off** dikh raha hai jiska jawaab aage ke data
  par depend karta hai.

> **Interview answer:** A greedy algorithm is correct when two properties hold. The greedy choice
> property says there exists an optimal solution that contains the first greedy choice — note that
> it's "there exists", not "every optimal solution contains it", and that phrasing is what makes
> the proof work. Optimal substructure says that after making that choice, what remains is a
> smaller instance of the same problem.
>
> Dynamic programming needs only the second property, which is why it explores all the choices.
> Greedy has both, so it can commit to one and never look back — that's the entire difference
> between the two paradigms.
>
> To prove it I use one of two arguments. The exchange argument takes an arbitrary optimal solution
> and transforms it step by step into the greedy one without ever making it worse. "Greedy stays
> ahead" uses induction to show the greedy partial solution is at least as good as any other after
> every step. If I can't sketch one of those in a couple of sentences, I don't trust the greedy and
> I write the DP instead — a correct slow answer beats a fast wrong one.

---

### The Exchange Argument

#### Kya hai

Greedy ko prove karne ka sabse standard tareeka: **koi bhi optimal solution lo, aur usme ek-ek
badlaav karke usse greedy solution bana do — har badlaav se answer kharaab nahi hona chahiye.**
*Analogy:* aap keh rahe ho "tumhara jo bhi best plan hai, main usme ek cheez badal doonga jisse
wo mera plan jaisa ho jaayega aur utna hi accha rahega — matlab mera plan bhi best hai."

#### Template — chaar steps

1. Maano `O` ek optimal solution hai jo greedy `G` se **alag** hai.
2. **Pehli jagah dhoondho** jahan dono alag hain (ye zaroori hai — "pehli" se induction chalta hai).
3. `O` mein us jagah **swap karo** taaki wo `G` se match kar jaaye.
4. Dikhao ki swap ke baad `O` **abhi bhi valid** hai aur **utna hi accha ya behtar** hai.

Nateeja: `G` jitne bhi points par `O` se alag tha, sab badle ja sakte hain bina kharaab kiye —
matlab `G` bhi optimal hai. ∎

**Step 4 ke do hisse dono zaroori hain.** Sirf "value kharaab nahi hui" kaafi nahi — swap ke baad
solution **feasible** bhi rehna chahiye (constraints toote nahi).

#### Worked example — activity selection

**Greedy:** sabse pehle **khatam hone wali** activity chuno.

**Proof:** maano `O` optimal hai aur usme pehli activity `a1` hai, jabki greedy `g1` chunta hai
jiska finish time sabse kam hai. To `finish(g1) <= finish(a1)`.

Ab `O` mein `a1` ko hata kar `g1` daal do. **Valid hai kya?** `O` ki doosri activity `a2` ka
start time `>= finish(a1) >= finish(g1)` hai — to `g1` uske saath clash nahi karti. **Count
badla?** Nahi, ek hataayi ek daali — count same. Matlab naya solution bhi optimal hai **aur
greedy choice include karta hai**. Yahi induction har step par lagao. ∎

#### Worked example 2 — job sequencing (deadline wala)

**Greedy:** profit ke ghatte order mein jobs dekho, har job ko uske deadline ke **sabse late
khaali slot** mein daalo.

**Exchange:** maano `O` mein job `x` (profit 100) reject hai par job `y` (profit 40) accept hai,
aur `x` ka koi valid slot `y` ke slot se compatible tha. `y` hata kar `x` daal do — deadline abhi
bhi satisfy hoti hai (kyunki hum `y` ka slot use kar rahe hain jo `x` ke deadline ke andar tha),
aur profit **60 badh gaya**. Matlab `O` optimal tha hi nahi — contradiction. **Isliye greedy ka
"zyada profit pehle" sahi hai.**

**"Sabse late slot" wala hissa alag se justify hota hai:** late slot bharne se pehle wale slots
khaali rehte hain, jo tight deadline wali jobs ke liye bache rehte hain. Early slot bharna kabhi
behtar nahi ho sakta.

#### Jab exchange argument **fail** hota hai — counterexample

**0/1 knapsack, ratio ke hisaab se greedy.** Items: `(w=10, v=60)`, `(w=20, v=100)`,
`(w=30, v=120)`. Capacity 50. Ratios: 6, 5, 4.

Greedy: item1 (10, 60) + item2 (20, 100) = 30 weight, 160 value. Bacha 20 weight, item3 (30) fit
nahi hota. **Total 160.**
Optimal: item2 + item3 = 50 weight, **220 value**.

**Exchange kyun fail hua?** Kyunki `O` mein se item3 hata kar item1 daalne se weight **badalta**
hai — hum "ek ke badle ek" swap nahi kar sakte, kyunki items indivisible hain aur weights alag
hain. Exchange argument tabhi chalta hai jab swap **feasibility todhe bina** ho sake. Fractional
knapsack mein ye chalta hai kyunki wahan hum **exactly `y-x` weight** exchange kar sakte hain.

**Yahi ek line yaad rakhne layak hai:** greedy tab tootta hai jab swap karne par
feasibility ya to tootti hai ya usse compensate karne mein value girti hai.

> **Interview answer:** The exchange argument is how I prove a greedy is optimal. I take an
> arbitrary optimal solution, find the first place where it differs from the greedy choice, and
> swap that element for the greedy one. Then I show two things: the modified solution is still
> feasible, and it's no worse than before. Repeating that transforms any optimal solution into the
> greedy one without loss, so the greedy must itself be optimal.
>
> For activity selection, the greedy picks the earliest finishing activity. If an optimal solution
> starts with a different activity, that one finishes no earlier, so replacing it with the greedy
> choice can't create a conflict with whatever came next, and the count is unchanged. Induction
> does the rest.
>
> Where it fails is just as instructive. In 0/1 knapsack the swap isn't weight-neutral — exchanging
> one item for another changes how much capacity is left, so feasibility breaks and the argument
> collapses. That's precisely why fractional knapsack is greedy and 0/1 is DP: divisibility is what
> makes the exchange legal.

---

### Activity Selection

#### Kya hai

Start-end times wali activities di hain; **maximum kitni activities** kar sakte ho bina overlap ke.
*Analogy:* ek conference room hai aur bees meeting requests — sabse zyada meetings kaise fit karein.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

**Finish time** se sort karo, aur har wo activity utha lo jiska start pichhli chuni hui activity
ke finish ke baad ho. Intuition: jaldi khatam hone wali activity **sabse zyada baaki time
chhodti hai**, aur count maximise karna hai — duration se koi matlab nahi.

#### Code

```python
def activity_selection(intervals):
    """(start, end) list se maximum non-overlapping activities."""
    if not intervals:                               # 1
        return []                                   # 2
    order = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[1])   # 3
    chosen = [order[0]]                             # 4
    last_end = order[0][1]                          # 5
    for s, e in order[1:]:                          # 6
        if s >= last_end:                           # 7
            chosen.append((s, e))                   # 8
            last_end = e                            # 9
    return chosen                                   # 10


def erase_overlap_intervals(intervals):
    """Kam se kam kitne intervals hataane padenge taaki koi overlap na bache."""
    if not intervals:                               # 11
        return 0                                    # 12
    order = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[1])   # 13
    kept, last_end = 1, order[0][1]                 # 14
    for s, e in order[1:]:                          # 15
        if s >= last_end:                           # 16
            kept += 1                               # 17
            last_end = e                            # 18
    return len(intervals) - kept                    # 19
```

**Line-by-line:**

3. **`key=x[1]` — end time se sort.** Start se sort karna galat hai (neeche counterexample),
   duration se sort karna bhi galat hai.
5. `last_end` hi poori state hai — pichhli chuni gayi activity ka end. Isse zyada kuchh yaad
   rakhne ki zaroorat nahi, aur yahi greedy ko O(n) banata hai.
7. `s >= last_end` — agar meetings back-to-back allowed hain (`[1,3]` aur `[3,5]` clash nahi).
   Agar strict gap chahiye to `s > last_end`.
11-19. **Same algorithm, ulta sawaal.** "Kitne hataao" = total minus "kitne rakh sakte ho".
   Interview mein ye do problems alag lagti hain, hain ek hi.

#### Compact dry run — `[(1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), (3,9), (5,9), (6,10), (8,11)]`

Sort by end: `(1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), (3,9), (5,9), (6,10), (8,11)`

| Activity | `s >= last_end`? | Chuna? | last_end |
|---|---|---|---|
| (1,4) | — (pehla) | haan | 4 |
| (3,5) | 3 >= 4? nahi | nahi | 4 |
| (0,6) | 0 >= 4? nahi | nahi | 4 |
| (5,7) | 5 >= 4? haan | **haan** | 7 |
| (3,9) | nahi | nahi | 7 |
| (5,9) | nahi | nahi | 7 |
| (6,10) | nahi | nahi | 7 |
| (8,11) | 8 >= 7? haan | **haan** | 11 |

Answer **3**: `(1,4), (5,7), (8,11)`.

#### Galat greedy — counterexample

**Start time se sort:** `(0, 100), (1, 2), (3, 4)`. Start se chalne par `(0,100)` pehle
aayegi aur baaki dono block ho jaayengi → answer 1. Sahi answer **2**.

**Shortest duration pehle:** `(0, 5), (4, 6), (5, 10)`. Sabse chhoti `(4,6)` hai, wo chunne par
baaki dono block → answer 1. End-time greedy `(0,5)` aur `(5,10)` deti hai → **2**.

#### Complexity

| | Value | Kyun |
|---|---|---|
| Time | **O(n log n)** | Sorting hi dominate karti hai; scan sirf O(n) |
| Space | O(1) extra (ya O(n) output ke liye) | Sirf `last_end` yaad hai |

Agar input **pehle se end-time sorted** aa raha ho (jaise database `ORDER BY end_time` se), to
**O(n)**.

> **Interview answer:** Activity selection asks for the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals.
> Sort by end time and greedily take any interval that starts at or after the last chosen one's
> end. Sorting dominates, so it's O(n log n) with O(1) extra state — just the last end time.
>
> Sorting by end time is the whole trick, and I can justify it two ways. Intuitively, finishing
> earliest leaves the most room for everything after. Formally, by an exchange argument: if some
> optimal solution starts with a different activity, that one finishes no earlier, so swapping in
> the earliest-finishing activity can't conflict with what follows and keeps the count identical.
>
> Sorting by start time or by duration both fail on small examples, and I'd expect to be asked for
> one. A single long interval starting at zero defeats start-time ordering; a short interval in the
> middle that straddles two others defeats duration ordering.
>
> The same algorithm answers "minimum intervals to remove so none overlap" — that's just the total
> minus the maximum you can keep, which catches people who treat them as separate problems.

### Fractional Knapsack

#### Kya hai

0/1 knapsack ka wo version jahan items ko **kaata ja sakta hai** — aadha item bhi le sakte ho,
aur value bhi aadhi milegi.
*Analogy:* chor bori mein sona, chandi aur gehun bhar raha hai — powder aur dhaatu ko tol kar
aadha bhi le sakta hai.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

Har item ka **value per unit weight** nikalo, us ratio ke ghatte order mein sort karo, aur bag
bharte jao. Jo aakhri item poora fit na ho, usko **fraction mein** le lo. Divisibility hi wo
cheez hai jo greedy ko yahan sahi banati hai — 0/1 mein ye nahi hai isliye wahan DP chahiye.

#### Code

```python
def fractional_knapsack(items, capacity):
    """items = [(weight, value), ...]. Maximum value, fractions allowed."""
    order = sorted(items, key=lambda it: it[1] / it[0], reverse=True)   # 1
    total = 0.0                                     # 2
    remaining = capacity                            # 3
    for w, v in order:                              # 4
        if remaining <= 0:                          # 5
            break                                   # 6
        take = min(w, remaining)                    # 7
        total += v * (take / w)                     # 8
        remaining -= take                           # 9
    return total                                    # 10
```

**Line-by-line:**

1. **Ratio `v/w` ke ghatte order mein sort** — yahi poora algorithm hai. `reverse=True` bhoolna
   sabse common bug hai (tab aap sabse bekaar items pehle bharoge).
5-6. Bag bhar gaya, ruk jao.
7. **`min(w, remaining)`** — ya to poora item, ya jitna bacha hai. Yahi ek line "fraction" handle
   karti hai; alag `if` ki zaroorat nahi.
8. `take/w` = kitna fraction liya, usi hisaab se value. Poora item ho to `take/w == 1`.

#### Compact dry run — items `[(10, 60), (20, 100), (30, 120)]`, capacity 50

Ratios: 6.0, 5.0, 4.0 — already sorted.

| Item | ratio | remaining (pehle) | take | value add | remaining (baad) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (10, 60) | 6.0 | 50 | 10 | 60 | 40 |
| (20, 100) | 5.0 | 40 | 20 | 100 | 20 |
| (30, 120) | 4.0 | 20 | **20 (2/3)** | **80** | 0 |

Total **240**. Wahi input 0/1 knapsack mein sirf **220** deta hai (`(20,100) + (30,120)`) —
kyunki wahan aakhri item ko kaata nahi ja sakta. **Yahi do problems ka farak hai.**

#### Complexity

| | Value | Kyun |
|---|---|---|
| Time | **O(n log n)** | Sorting; scan O(n) |
| Time (theoretical best) | **O(n)** | Quickselect se ratio ka median nikaal kar partition — median-of-medians wala approach |
| Space | O(1) extra | Sirf running total |

**Floating point ka dhyaan:** `v/w` compare karte waqt precision issues aa sakte hain. Safe
compare: `v1 * w2 > v2 * w1` (cross-multiplication, integers mein).

> **Interview answer:** Fractional knapsack is the greedy sibling of 0/1 knapsack. Because items
> can be split, I sort by value-to-weight ratio descending and fill the bag, taking a fraction of
> whichever item doesn't fit whole. That's O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
>
> The exchange argument is clean here: if an optimal solution takes less of the highest-ratio item
> than it could, it must be taking some weight of a lower-ratio item instead. Swapping that exact
> weight over keeps the bag equally full and never decreases the value. Because the weights match
> exactly, feasibility is preserved — and that is exactly what fails in 0/1 knapsack, where items
> are indivisible and swapping changes the remaining capacity.
>
> On the same input — weights 10, 20, 30 with values 60, 100, 120 and a capacity of 50 — greedy
> gives 240 fractionally but only 160 if you apply it to the 0/1 version, where the true optimum is
> 220. That example is worth memorising because it demonstrates both algorithms in one breath.
>
> A detail I'd mention: comparing ratios as floats can misbehave, so I cross-multiply integers
> instead.

---

### Huffman Coding

#### Kya hai

Characters ko **variable-length binary codes** do — jo character zyada baar aata hai use chhota
code, kam aane wale ko lamba — taaki total encoded size minimum ho.
*Analogy:* Morse code mein `E` (sabse common letter) ek dot hai aur `Q` chaar symbols ka —
wahi idea, par data se automatically nikaala gaya.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

Har character ko ek leaf node banao jiska weight = uski frequency. Baar baar **do sabse halke
nodes** utha kar unhe ek naye parent ke neeche jodo (parent ka weight = dono ka sum). Jab ek node
bache, wo root hai — left edge `0`, right edge `1`, aur har leaf tak ka path uska code hai.
Sabse zyada frequency wala character sabse upar rehta hai, isliye uska code sabse chhota.

#### Code

```python
import heapq
from collections import Counter


def huffman_codes(text):
    """Har character ka prefix-free binary code."""
    freq = Counter(text)                            # 1
    if len(freq) == 1:                              # 2
        return {next(iter(freq)): "0"}              # 3
    heap = [[w, i, {ch: ""}] for i, (ch, w) in enumerate(freq.items())]   # 4
    heapq.heapify(heap)                             # 5
    counter = len(heap)                             # 6
    while len(heap) > 1:                            # 7
        w1, _, left = heapq.heappop(heap)           # 8
        w2, _, right = heapq.heappop(heap)          # 9
        merged = {}                                 # 10
        for ch, code in left.items():               # 11
            merged[ch] = "0" + code                 # 12
        for ch, code in right.items():              # 13
            merged[ch] = "1" + code                 # 14
        heapq.heappush(heap, [w1 + w2, counter, merged])   # 15
        counter += 1                                # 16
    return heap[0][2]                               # 17


def encoded_length(text):
    """Huffman ke baad total bits."""
    codes = huffman_codes(text)                     # 18
    return sum(len(codes[ch]) for ch in text)       # 19
```

**Line-by-line:**

2-3. **Edge case:** sirf ek unique character ho to loop kabhi nahi chalega aur code khaali reh
   jaayega. Manually `"0"` do.
4. Har entry `[weight, tiebreak, {char: code}]`. **`counter` isliye chahiye** kyunki weights tie
   hone par Python dict compare karne ki koshish karega aur `TypeError` dega.
8-9. **Do sabse halke** — heap ka poora point yahi hai.
11-14. Left subtree ke saare codes ke aage `0`, right ke aage `1`. **Prefix aage lagta hai,
   peeche nahi** — kyunki hum neeche se upar bana rahe hain.
17. Ek hi node bacha = root, uska dict hi saare codes hai.

#### Compact dry run — `"aaabbc"` → freq `a:3, b:2, c:1`

| Step | Heap (weights) | Action |
|---|---|---|
| init | 1(c), 2(b), 3(a) | — |
| 1 | pop 1, 2 → push 3 | `c="0"`, `b="1"` under node(3) |
| 2 | 3(a), 3(bc) | pop dono → push 6 |
| final | 6 | `a="0"`, `c="10"`, `b="11"` |

Bits: `a`×3 = 3, `b`×2 = 4, `c`×1 = 2 → **9 bits**. Fixed 2-bit code se 12 bits lagte — **25%
bachat**.

#### Complexity

| | Value | Kyun |
|---|---|---|
| Time | **O(n log n)** | `n` unique characters, har merge par do pops + ek push, sab log n |
| Space | O(n) | Heap + code table |
| Optimality | Provable | Exchange argument: do sabse kam frequency wale characters **hamesha** sabse gehre level par bhaai-behen ban sakte hain |

**Prefix-free property:** koi bhi code kisi doosre ka prefix nahi hota, kyunki saare characters
**leaves** par hain — leaf tak pahunchne ke baad path khatam. Isi wajah se decoding bina separator
ke ho jaati hai.

> **Interview answer:** Huffman coding builds an optimal prefix-free code from character
> frequencies. I put every character in a min-heap keyed by frequency, repeatedly pop the two
> lightest nodes, merge them under a new parent whose weight is their sum, and push it back. When
> one node remains it's the root; labelling left edges zero and right edges one gives each leaf its
> code. That's O(n log n) for n distinct symbols.
>
> The greedy choice is that the two least frequent characters can always be placed as siblings at
> the deepest level of some optimal tree — if they weren't, swapping them with whatever is down
> there would reduce the total cost, because you'd be moving smaller weights to longer paths.
>
> The property that makes it usable is prefix-freeness: every character sits at a leaf, so no
> code is a prefix of another and the decoder never needs delimiters. It's the entropy-coding stage
> inside DEFLATE, so it's running every time you gzip a response body.
>
> Two implementation details I watch for: a single distinct character produces an empty code unless
> special-cased, and heap entries need a tiebreaker so equal frequencies don't force Python to
> compare the payloads.

### Job Sequencing with Deadlines

#### Kya hai

Har job ka ek **deadline** aur ek **profit** hai; har job ko **ek unit time** lagta hai aur ek
time par ek hi job chal sakti hai. Maximum profit kaise?
*Analogy:* aaj shaam tak paanch clients ke kaam nipatane hain, har ek ka alag deadline aur alag
paisa — kaunse kaam lo.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

Profit ke **ghatte order** mein jobs dekho. Har job ke liye uske deadline se **peeche ki taraf**
pehla khaali slot dhoondho aur wahan daal do. Late slot bharne se early slots un jobs ke liye
bache rehte hain jinki deadline tight hai.

#### Code

```python
def job_sequencing(jobs):
    """jobs = [(job_id, deadline, profit)]. Simple O(n^2) version."""
    order = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[2], reverse=True)   # 1
    max_dl = max(j[1] for j in jobs)                # 2
    slots = [None] * (max_dl + 1)                   # 3
    profit = 0                                      # 4
    for jid, dl, p in order:                        # 5
        t = min(dl, max_dl)                         # 6
        while t > 0 and slots[t] is not None:       # 7
            t -= 1                                  # 8
        if t > 0:                                   # 9
            slots[t] = jid                          # 10
            profit += p                             # 11
    return profit, [s for s in slots if s]          # 12


def job_sequencing_dsu(jobs):
    """O(n log n) — union find se agla khaali slot O(alpha) mein."""
    order = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[2], reverse=True)   # 13
    max_dl = max(j[1] for j in jobs)                # 14
    parent = list(range(max_dl + 1))                # 15

    def find(x):                                    # 16
        while parent[x] != x:                       # 17
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]           # 18
            x = parent[x]                           # 19
        return x                                    # 20

    profit, picked = 0, []                          # 21
    for jid, dl, p in order:                        # 22
        slot = find(min(dl, max_dl))                # 23
        if slot > 0:                                # 24
            parent[slot] = slot - 1                 # 25
            profit += p                             # 26
            picked.append(jid)                      # 27
    return profit, picked                           # 28
```

**Line-by-line:**

1. **Profit ghatte order** — exchange argument isi ko justify karta hai (pichhla section).
3. Slots `1..max_dl`; index `0` jaanbujh kar unused rakha hai taaki "koi slot nahi mila" ka
   matlab `t == 0` ho jaaye.
6-8. **Deadline se peeche chalo**, pehla khaali slot lo. Aage nahi — deadline cross nahi kar sakte.
9-11. Slot mila to job accept.

13-28. **Optimised.** `parent[t]` = "`t` ya usse pehle ka pehla khaali slot".
23. `find` seedha khaali slot deta hai, `while` loop ke bina.
25. Slot bhar gaya to usko `slot-1` par point kara do — agli baar `find` khud aage skip kar dega.
   **Yahi trick O(n²) ko O(n log n) banati hai.**

#### Compact dry run — `[(a,2,100), (b,1,19), (c,2,27), (d,1,25), (e,3,15)]`

Profit se sort: `a(2,100), c(2,27), d(1,25), b(1,19), e(3,15)`

| Job | dl | Slot dhoondha | Result | Profit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a | 2 | 2 khaali | slot 2 | 100 |
| c | 2 | 2 bhara → 1 khaali | slot 1 | 127 |
| d | 1 | 1 bhara → 0 | **reject** | 127 |
| b | 1 | 1 bhara → 0 | **reject** | 127 |
| e | 3 | 3 khaali | slot 3 | **142** |

Answer **142**, jobs `c, a, e` (slots 1, 2, 3).

#### Complexity

| Version | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| Simple | **O(n log n + n·D)** | O(D) slots |
| Union-find | **O(n log n)** | O(D) |

`D` = maximum deadline. Agar `D` bada ho aur jobs kam, to union-find wala clearly behtar hai.

> **Interview answer:** Job sequencing with deadlines gives each unit-length job a deadline and a
> profit, one machine, and asks for maximum profit. The greedy is: sort by profit descending, and
> schedule each job in the latest free slot at or before its deadline.
>
> Both halves need justification. Taking higher profit first follows from an exchange argument — if
> an optimal schedule rejects a job it could have run in place of a less profitable one, swapping
> them keeps every deadline satisfied and raises the profit, so it wasn't optimal. Filling the
> latest slot is the second half: it leaves earlier slots free for jobs with tighter deadlines, and
> can never be worse than filling an earlier one.
>
> The naive slot search is O(n times D). I can get it to near O(n log n) with a disjoint set union
> where each slot points to the first free slot at or before it — when I fill a slot I union it
> into slot minus one, so the next lookup skips the filled run in nearly constant time. That DSU
> trick shows up in several scheduling problems and is usually what the interviewer is fishing for
> once the basic greedy is on the board.

---

### Interval Scheduling and Merging

#### Kya hai

Intervals ka ek family of problems — merge karna, insert karna, overlap ginna, minimum rooms
nikaalna. Sab ek hi do ideas par khade hain: **sort karo**, aur **sirf ek boundary yaad rakho**.
*Analogy:* calendar par blocks; kabhi unhe jodna hai, kabhi ginna hai ki ek waqt par kitne
overlap ho rahe hain.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

**Merging ke liye start se sort karo** — tabhi overlapping intervals adjacent aate hain.
**Counting/rooms ke liye events banao** (`+1` on start, `-1` on end) aur time ke order mein
chalo — running sum ka maximum hi answer hai. **Selection ke liye end se sort karo** (pichhla
section).

#### Code

```python
def merge_intervals(intervals):
    """Overlapping intervals ko jodo. Start se sort."""
    if not intervals:                               # 1
        return []                                   # 2
    order = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[0])   # 3
    out = [list(order[0])]                          # 4
    for s, e in order[1:]:                          # 5
        if s <= out[-1][1]:                         # 6
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)         # 7
        else:                                       # 8
            out.append([s, e])                      # 9
    return out                                      # 10


def min_meeting_rooms(intervals):
    """Ek waqt par maximum kitne overlap — sweep line."""
    events = []                                     # 11
    for s, e in intervals:                          # 12
        events.append((s, 1))                       # 13
        events.append((e, -1))                      # 14
    events.sort()                                   # 15
    active = best = 0                               # 16
    for _, delta in events:                         # 17
        active += delta                             # 18
        if active > best:                           # 19
            best = active                           # 20
    return best                                     # 21


def insert_interval(intervals, new):
    """Sorted non-overlapping list mein ek naya interval daalo. O(n)."""
    out, i, n = [], 0, len(intervals)               # 22
    s, e = new                                      # 23
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < s:            # 24
        out.append(intervals[i])                    # 25
        i += 1                                      # 26
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= e:           # 27
        s = min(s, intervals[i][0])                 # 28
        e = max(e, intervals[i][1])                 # 29
        i += 1                                      # 30
    out.append((s, e))                              # 31
    out.extend(intervals[i:])                       # 32
    return out                                      # 33
```

**Line-by-line:**

3. **Start se sort** — merging ke liye. End se sort karoge to `[1,10]` aur `[2,3]` alag alag
   jagah pahunch jaayenge.
6. `s <= out[-1][1]` — touch karte intervals (`[1,3]`, `[3,5]`) merge honge. Sirf strict overlap
   chahiye to `<` kar do.
7. **`max` zaroori hai** — `[1,10]` ke baad `[2,3]` aane par end ko 3 mat kar dena. Ye sabse
   common bug hai.

13-15. `(time, +1)` aur `(time, -1)`. **Sort mein `-1` pehle aata hai** jab time barabar ho
   (kyunki `-1 < 1`) — matlab ek meeting jis waqt khatam hoti hai usi waqt doosri shuru ho sakti
   hai, same room mein. Agar cleanup time chahiye to end event ko `(e, 1)` se pehle force karna
   padega.
18-20. Running count ka maximum = minimum rooms.

24-26. Naye interval se **poori tarah pehle** wale, jaise ke taise.
27-30. **Overlap karne wale sab absorb** karo, boundaries ko stretch karte hue.
31-32. Merged interval daalo, phir baaki.

#### Compact dry run — `min_meeting_rooms([(0,30), (5,10), (15,20)])`

Events sorted: `(0,+1), (5,+1), (10,-1), (15,+1), (20,-1), (30,-1)`

| Event | active | best |
|---|---|---|
| (0,+1) | 1 | 1 |
| (5,+1) | **2** | **2** |
| (10,-1) | 1 | 2 |
| (15,+1) | 2 | 2 |
| (20,-1) | 1 | 2 |
| (30,-1) | 0 | 2 |

Answer **2 rooms**.

#### Complexity

| Problem | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| Merge | **O(n log n)** | O(n) output |
| Min rooms (sweep) | **O(n log n)** | O(n) events |
| Insert into sorted list | **O(n)** | O(n) — sorting ki zaroorat nahi |

#### Kaunsa sort — ek line ka rule

| Sawaal | Sort by |
|---|---|
| Maximum non-overlapping **count** | **end** |
| Intervals **merge** karo | **start** |
| Minimum **rooms** / max overlap | **events**, ya start-heap |
| Sorted list mein **insert** | koi nahi — linear scan |

> **Interview answer:** Interval problems are one family with one decision at the front: what do I
> sort by. If I need the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals, I sort by end time. If I need
> to merge them, I sort by start time, because only then are overlapping intervals adjacent. If I
> need the maximum concurrency — minimum meeting rooms — I don't sort intervals at all, I turn each
> into a plus-one event at its start and a minus-one at its end, sort the events, and track the
> running maximum.
>
> Merging is O(n log n) and the classic bug is extending the current interval's end to the new
> interval's end rather than to the max of the two, which silently truncates when a short interval
> sits inside a long one.
>
> Tie handling is worth stating explicitly: when one meeting ends exactly as another begins, whether
> they share a room depends on whether the end event sorts before the start event. I'd confirm that
> convention with the interviewer rather than assume it.
>
> Inserting into an already-sorted, non-overlapping list is a special case that needs no sort at
> all — a single linear pass in three phases: before, overlapping, after.

---

### When Greedy Looks Right and Is Wrong

Ye section deliberately code ke bina hai. Greedy ka asli khatra ye hai ki **wo chhote test cases
par pass ho jaata hai** — aap confident ho jaate ho, aur production mein ya interview ke doosre
example par toot jaata hai.

#### Counterexample 1 — Coin change

**Greedy:** hamesha sabse bada coin lo jo fit ho.
**Coins `[1, 3, 4]`, amount `6`.**

| Approach | Choices | Coins |
|---|---|---|
| Greedy | 4, phir 1, phir 1 | **3** |
| Optimal | 3, 3 | **2** |

**Kyun toota:** `4` lene se `2` bacha, jo sirf `1+1` se banta hai. `4` ne ek **badi jagah** to
bhari par **remainder ko kharaab** kar diya. Local best ne future ko constrain kar diya — yahi
greedy ke fail hone ki asli definition hai.

**Dhyaan dene layak:** Indian currency (`1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100`) aur US currency par greedy
**kaam karta hai**, kyunki ye "canonical coin systems" hain. Isliye aap zindagi bhar greedy se
change dete aaye ho aur kabhi galat nahi hua — aur isliye interview mein greedy pehla instinct
banta hai. **Arbitrary denominations par wo instinct galat hai.**

#### Counterexample 2 — 0/1 Knapsack

**Greedy:** highest value/weight ratio pehle.
**Items `(w=10,v=60), (w=20,v=100), (w=30,v=120)`, capacity `50`.**

| Approach | Items | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Greedy (ratio) | 10 + 20 = 30 wt | **160** (20 wt barbaad) |
| Optimal | 20 + 30 = 50 wt | **220** |

**Kyun toota:** indivisibility. Greedy ne 20 units capacity khaali chhod di kyunki bacha hua item
fit nahi hua. Fractional version mein yahi greedy **perfect** hai — **ek shabd (`fractional`) poora
paradigm badal deta hai.**

#### Counterexample 3 — Longest path in a graph

**Greedy:** har node par sabse bhaari edge lo.

```
A --10--> B --1--> D
A --2---> C --50-> D
```

Greedy `A→B→D` = 11. Optimal `A→C→D` = **52**. Shortest path ke liye Dijkstra greedy hai aur
correct hai; **longest path ke liye greedy correct nahi hai** aur asal mein longest path
NP-hard hai. **Same graph, ulta objective, bilkul alag difficulty.**

#### Counterexample 4 — Task assignment ("sabse jaldi wale ko pehle")

Do workers, tasks `[8, 4, 4, 4]` hours. Greedy "sabse bada task pehle, sabse khaali worker ko":
W1 gets 8, W2 gets 4+4+4=12 → makespan **12**. Optimal: W1 = 8+4 = 12, W2 = 4+4 = 8 → **12**.
Yahan greedy sahi nikla. Ab tasks `[7, 6, 5, 4, 3]`: greedy 7+4+3=14 / 6+5=11 → **14**;
optimal 7+6=13 / 5+4+3=12 → **13**. **Ek input par pass, doosre par fail** — aur yahi sabse
khatarnaak pattern hai, kyunki aapka pehla test case aksar aasan hota hai.

#### Ek chhoti checklist — greedy likhne se pehle

| Sawaal | Agar haan |
|---|---|
| Kya ek choice baad ki choices ki **feasibility** badalti hai? | Greedy shaq ke ghere mein |
| Kya items **indivisible** hain aur capacity bandhi hai? | Zyaadatar DP |
| Kya main **exchange argument** do line mein bol sakta hoon? | Greedy likho |
| Kya maine sirf **do** test cases par check kiya? | Teesra banao, jaanbujh kar adversarial |
| Kya problem "maximum/minimum **count**" maang rahi hai, values nahi? | Greedy ka chance zyada |

#### Adversarial test case kaise banayein

Ye QA wali skill hai aur interview mein bohot achhi lagti hai:

1. **Ek bada element daalo jo pehle aata hai** — greedy usse utha lega aur baaki block ho jaayenge
   (activity selection ka `(0, 100)`).
2. **Do medium elements banao jinka sum ek bade se behtar ho** — coin change `[1,3,4]` par `6`.
3. **Capacity aisi rakho ki greedy ke baad thoda sa space bache** jo waste ho — knapsack wala 20.
4. **Ties daalo** — barabar values par greedy ka tie-break aksar undefined hota hai aur wahi bug
   ban jaata hai.

#### Interview mein sahi behaviour

Greedy dikhe to bolo: **"My first instinct is greedy — sort by X and take the best each time. Let
me test that against a case designed to break it before I commit."** Phir jaanbujh kar ek
counterexample banane ki koshish karo. Do nateeje hain aur dono achhe hain: ya to greedy tootega
(aur aapne DP par time bacha liya), ya nahi tootega (aur ab aapke paas confidence + ek proof
sketch hai). **Interviewer ko yahi process dekhna hai, sirf answer nahi.**

> **Interview answer:** Greedy is the paradigm I trust least without a proof, because it passes
> small tests and fails on the interesting ones. The canonical failure is coin change: with
> denominations 1, 3 and 4 and a target of 6, greedy takes a 4 and needs three coins, while the
> optimum is two 3s. It fails because taking the locally largest coin leaves a remainder that's
> expensive to fill — the local choice constrained the future.
>
> The reason the instinct is so strong is that real currency systems are canonical, so greedy does
> work on rupees and dollars. That's a habit, not a proof.
>
> The same shape appears elsewhere: 0/1 knapsack by value-to-weight ratio wastes capacity because
> items are indivisible, and greedy on longest path fails outright while the identical greedy on
> shortest path is Dijkstra and is correct. Before committing I ask whether one choice changes what
> remains feasible; if it does, I go to DP. And I deliberately construct an adversarial case — one
> big early element, or two medium elements that beat one large one — rather than trusting the
> examples I was given.

## Part 7: String Algorithms

String matching un chand jagahon mein se hai jahan ek algorithm ka farak **naap kar** dikh jaata
hai. Naive matching 10 MB log file mein ek pattern dhoondhne mein minutes le sakta hai; KMP
seconds mein kar dega. Aur QA mein ye roz kaam aata hai — logs, HTML, API responses, diffs.

Yahan ek cheez shuru mein saaf kar dena zaroori hai: **Python ka `in` operator pehle se optimised
hai** (CPython mein a mixed Boyer-Moore-Horspool / two-way algorithm). To in algorithms ko aap
production mein rarely likhoge — inko seekhne ki wajah ye hai ki interview mein poochhe jaate hain
aur inke andar ke ideas (prefix function, rolling hash) doosri jagah reuse hote hain.

---

### Naive Pattern Matching

#### Kya hai

Text ke **har position** par pattern ko rakh kar character-by-character compare karo.
*Analogy:* ek chaabi ke gucchhe se har chaabi taala mein daal kar dekhna — koi chaturai nahi,
sirf mehnat.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

`i` ko `0` se `n - m` tak ghumao. Har `i` par pattern ke saare characters match karo; ek bhi
mismatch mile to turant break karo aur `i + 1` par phir se **shuru se** compare karo. Yahi
"shuru se" wali baat hi iski kamzori hai — pichhle comparisons se jo information mili thi, wo
phenk di jaati hai.

#### Code

```python
def naive_search(text, pattern):
    """Saare occurrences ke starting indices."""
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)                  # 1
    if m == 0 or m > n:                             # 2
        return []                                   # 3
    result = []                                     # 4
    for i in range(n - m + 1):                      # 5
        j = 0                                       # 6
        while j < m and text[i + j] == pattern[j]:  # 7
            j += 1                                  # 8
        if j == m:                                  # 9
            result.append(i)                        # 10
    return result                                   # 11


def naive_search_slice(text, pattern):
    """Wahi cheez, Python slicing se — chhota par same complexity."""
    m = len(text) - len(pattern) + 1                # 12
    return [i for i in range(m)
            if text[i:i + len(pattern)] == pattern]  # 13
```

**Line-by-line:**

2-3. Khaali pattern ya text se lamba pattern — edge cases jo interview mein poochhe jaate hain.
5. **`n - m + 1` positions** — isse aage pattern text se bahar nikal jaayega. `n` likh dena
   classic off-by-one hai.
7-8. Jab tak match ho rahi hai aage badho.
9-10. `j` poore `m` tak pahuncha = poora pattern mil gaya.

12-13. Slicing wala version padhne mein saaf hai par **har slice ek naya string banata hai**
   (O(m) copy), to constant factor kharaab hai — chhote inputs par phir bhi tez chalta hai
   kyunki comparison C level par hota hai.

#### Compact dry run — `text = "AABAACAADAABAABA"`, `pattern = "AABA"`

| i | Compare | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | A✓A✓B✓A✓ | **match at 0** |
| 1 | A✓ A✗(B vs A) | fail, 2 comparisons |
| 2 | B✗ | fail, 1 comparison |
| 3 | A✓A✓C✗ | fail, 3 |
| ... | | |
| 9 | A✓A✓B✓A✓ | **match at 9** |
| 12 | A✓A✓B✓A✓ | **match at 12** |

Matches: `[0, 9, 12]`.

#### Worst case — kab sach mein O(n·m) hota hai

`text = "AAAAAAAAAB"`, `pattern = "AAAB"`. Har position par pehle teen `A` match honge aur
chautha character fail karega — matlab har shift par **poora m** kaam. Ye pattern real logs mein
bhi banta hai: repeated whitespace, `====` separators, base64 padding.

#### Complexity

| Case | Time | Kyun |
|---|---|---|
| Best | **O(n)** | Har position par pehla hi character mismatch |
| Average (random text) | **O(n)** | Expected comparisons per position constant hoti hain |
| Worst | **O(n·m)** | `n-m+1` positions × `m` comparisons |
| Space | **O(1)** | Koi extra structure nahi |

**Yahi wajah hai ki naive bura nahi hai** — random-ish text par wo practically linear hai aur
zero preprocessing leta hai. KMP ka faayda tabhi milta hai jab pattern mein **khud ke andar
repetition** ho.

> **Interview answer:** Naive pattern matching slides the pattern across every starting position
> and compares characters until a mismatch. It's O(n times m) in the worst case, O(1) space, and
> needs no preprocessing.
>
> The worst case needs a highly repetitive text and pattern — something like a long run of As with
> a B at the end of the pattern — because only then does every alignment do near-m work before
> failing. On typical English or log text the expected work per position is a small constant, so it
> behaves close to linear, which is why it's a perfectly reasonable answer for short patterns.
>
> Its real weakness is that it throws away information. After matching three characters and failing
> on the fourth, it restarts from scratch one position over, even though those three characters
> already told it something about the text. That discarded information is exactly what KMP captures
> in its prefix table, and framing it that way is how I'd motivate KMP as the next step.

---

### KMP

#### Kya hai

Knuth-Morris-Pratt — mismatch hone par text pointer ko **kabhi peeche nahi le jaata**; pattern ko
kitna aage khiskana hai ye ek precomputed table se aata hai.
*Analogy:* aapko pata hai ki `"AABA"` ke aakhir mein bhi `"A"` hai aur shuru mein bhi `"A"` — to
fail hone par poora shuru se nahi, us `"A"` ke baad se continue karo.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

Pehle pattern ka **LPS array** banao: `lps[i]` = `pattern[0..i]` ka sabse lamba proper prefix jo
suffix bhi ho. Phir matching ke waqt jab `pattern[j]` mismatch kare, `j = lps[j-1]` kar do —
matlab utne characters hum **already match kar chuke hain**, unhe dobara compare mat karo. `i`
kabhi decrement nahi hota, isliye text ek hi baar padha jaata hai.

#### Code

```python
def build_lps(pattern):
    """lps[i] = pattern[0..i] ka longest proper prefix jo suffix bhi ho."""
    m = len(pattern)                                # 1
    lps = [0] * m                                   # 2
    length = 0                                      # 3
    i = 1                                           # 4
    while i < m:                                    # 5
        if pattern[i] == pattern[length]:           # 6
            length += 1                             # 7
            lps[i] = length                         # 8
            i += 1                                  # 9
        elif length > 0:                            # 10
            length = lps[length - 1]                # 11
        else:                                       # 12
            lps[i] = 0                              # 13
            i += 1                                  # 14
    return lps                                      # 15


def kmp_search(text, pattern):
    """Saare occurrences. O(n + m)."""
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)                  # 16
    if m == 0 or m > n:                             # 17
        return []                                   # 18
    lps = build_lps(pattern)                        # 19
    result = []                                     # 20
    i = j = 0                                       # 21
    while i < n:                                    # 22
        if text[i] == pattern[j]:                   # 23
            i += 1                                  # 24
            j += 1                                  # 25
            if j == m:                              # 26
                result.append(i - m)                # 27
                j = lps[j - 1]                      # 28
        elif j > 0:                                 # 29
            j = lps[j - 1]                          # 30
        else:                                       # 31
            i += 1                                  # 32
    return result                                   # 33
```

**Line-by-line:**

3-4. `lps[0]` hamesha `0` hai (proper prefix khud poori string nahi ho sakti), isliye `i` `1` se.
6-9. Match — current prefix-suffix length badhao aur record karo.
10-11. **Ye poore algorithm ki sabse gehri line hai.** Mismatch hua par `length > 0` — matlab
   hum chhote prefix-suffix par fall back kar sakte hain. `length = lps[length-1]` recursively
   agla candidate deta hai, bina `i` ko hilaye.
12-14. `length == 0` — koi fallback nahi bacha, `lps[i] = 0`.

23-25. Match, dono aage.
26-28. **Poora pattern mil gaya.** `j = lps[j-1]` karke **overlapping matches** bhi milte hain
   (`"AAA"` mein `"AA"` do baar). `j = 0` karoge to overlapping chhoot jaayenge.
29-30. Mismatch par **sirf `j` peeche jaata hai, `i` nahi.** Yahi O(n) guarantee hai.
31-32. `j` already 0 hai — text mein ek kadam aage badho.

#### Compact dry run — LPS of `"AABAACAABAA"`

| i | char | length | lps |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | B | 0 (fallback) | 0 |
| 3 | A | 1 | 1 |
| 4 | A | 2 | 2 |
| 5 | C | 0 | 0 |
| 6 | A | 1 | 1 |
| 7 | A | 2 | 2 |
| 8 | B | 3 | 3 |
| 9 | A | 4 | 4 |
| 10 | A | 5 | **5** |

`lps = [0,1,0,1,2,0,1,2,3,4,5]`. Aakhri `5` ka matlab: `"AABAA"` shuru mein bhi hai aur aakhir
mein bhi.

#### Complexity

| | Value | Kyun |
|---|---|---|
| Preprocessing | **O(m)** | `i` kabhi peeche nahi jaata; `length` har step par max 1 badhta hai aur total ghatna badhne se zyada nahi ho sakta |
| Search | **O(n)** | `i` monotonically badhta hai; `j` bhi total mein `n` se zyada nahi ghat sakta |
| Total | **O(n + m)** | |
| Space | **O(m)** | LPS array |

**Amortised argument:** `j` har match par `+1` hota hai (max `n` baar), aur har fallback par
**ghatta** hai. Ghatne ka total badhne ke total se zyada nahi ho sakta — isliye fallbacks bhi
kul milakar `O(n)` hain, chahe ek iteration mein kai baar chalein.

> **Interview answer:** KMP finds all occurrences in O(n plus m) with O(m) extra space, and the key
> property is that the text pointer never moves backwards.
>
> It preprocesses the pattern into an LPS array, where lps[i] is the length of the longest proper
> prefix of the pattern's first i-plus-one characters that is also a suffix. When a mismatch happens
> at pattern position j, instead of restarting, I set j to lps[j-1] — those characters are already
> known to match, so re-comparing them is wasted work.
>
> The linearity argument is amortised, and it's worth stating properly: the text index only ever
> increases, and j increases by at most one per step, so the total amount j can decrease across all
> fallbacks is bounded by the total it increased. That's why the inner while loop doesn't make it
> quadratic.
>
> One detail: after a full match I reset j to lps[m-1] rather than zero, which is what lets it find
> overlapping occurrences. The LPS array is also independently useful — the shortest repeating unit
> of a string is n minus lps of the last index, when that divides n.

---

### Rabin Karp

#### Kya hai

Pattern aur har window ka **hash** compare karo; hash match hone par hi asli characters check
karo.
*Analogy:* do badi files ko compare karne se pehle unka checksum compare karna — checksum alag
hai to file dekhne ki zaroorat hi nahi.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

Ek **rolling hash** use hota hai: window ek kadam aage khiskane par poora dobara hash karne ki
zaroorat nahi — bas pehla character ka contribution ghatao, naya character jodo. Isse har shift
O(1) ho jaata hai. Hash barabar hone par bhi **string compare karna zaroori hai** (collision ho
sakti hai).

#### Code

```python
def rabin_karp(text, pattern, base=256, mod=1_000_000_007):
    """Saare occurrences. Average O(n + m), worst O(n*m)."""
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)                  # 1
    if m == 0 or m > n:                             # 2
        return []                                   # 3
    high = pow(base, m - 1, mod)                    # 4
    ph = th = 0                                     # 5
    for k in range(m):                              # 6
        ph = (ph * base + ord(pattern[k])) % mod    # 7
        th = (th * base + ord(text[k])) % mod       # 8
    result = []                                     # 9
    for i in range(n - m + 1):                      # 10
        if ph == th and text[i:i + m] == pattern:   # 11
            result.append(i)                        # 12
        if i < n - m:                               # 13
            th = (th - ord(text[i]) * high) % mod   # 14
            th = (th * base + ord(text[i + m])) % mod   # 15
    return result                                   # 16
```

**Line-by-line:**

4. `base^(m-1) mod p` — nikalte waqt sabse aage wale character ka place value. **`pow` ke teen
   arguments** modular exponentiation karte hain, O(log m) mein.
6-8. Dono initial hashes ek saath — polynomial hash: `c0·b^(m-1) + c1·b^(m-2) + … + cm-1`.
11. **`ph == th` ke baad bhi actual compare** — ye line hatana sabse badi galti hai. Hash match
   hona sirf **candidate** deta hai, proof nahi.
14. Sabse aage wala character hatao (`ord(text[i]) * high`).
15. Baaki ko ek place shift karo (`* base`) aur naya character jodo. **Ye do lines mil kar
   rolling hash hain.** Python ka `%` negative numbers ko bhi sahi handle karta hai, isliye
   line 14 ke baad extra `+ mod` ki zaroorat nahi (C++ mein hoti hai).

#### Compact dry run — `text = "ABCDE"`, `pattern = "CD"`, chhota base=10, mod=997

`ph = ord('C')*10 + ord('D') = 670 + 68 = 738`

| i | window | th | Match? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | AB | 65·10+66 = 716 | nahi |
| 1 | BC | (716 - 650)·10 + 67 = 727 | nahi |
| 2 | CD | (727 - 660)·10 + 68 = **738** | **haan** → verify → match at 2 |
| 3 | DE | (738 - 680)·10 + 69 = 649 | nahi |

#### Complexity

| Case | Time | Kyun |
|---|---|---|
| Preprocessing | O(m) | Dono hashes |
| Average | **O(n + m)** | Har shift O(1); collisions bohot kam |
| Worst | **O(n·m)** | Har window par hash match par string alag — adversarial input, ya bekaar hash |
| Space | **O(1)** | Sirf do integers |

**Worst case kab:** agar attacker ko `base` aur `mod` pata ho to wo jaanbujh kar colliding
strings bana sakta hai. Isliye security-sensitive jagah par **random base** chunna chahiye.

#### Kab Rabin-Karp KMP se behtar hai

**Multiple patterns ek saath dhoondhne mein.** Agar 1000 patterns hain jinki length same hai, to
unke hashes ek `set` mein daal do aur text par ek hi pass mein saare check ho jaayenge —
**O(n + total pattern length)**. KMP ke liye 1000 alag automata banane padte. **2D pattern
matching** aur **plagiarism detection** (document ke saare k-length substrings ke hashes) bhi
isi par khade hain.

> **Interview answer:** Rabin-Karp compares hashes instead of characters. I compute a polynomial
> rolling hash of the pattern and of the first window, then slide: subtract the leading character's
> contribution, multiply by the base, add the new character. Each shift is O(1), so the average
> case is O(n plus m) with constant extra space.
>
> Two things I always state. First, a hash match is only a candidate — I still compare the actual
> substring, because collisions exist. Skipping that verification is the classic bug and it makes
> the algorithm silently wrong. Second, the worst case is O(n times m) when every window collides,
> which an adversary can construct if the base and modulus are known, so I'd randomise them if the
> input is untrusted.
>
> Where it genuinely beats KMP is multiple patterns of the same length: put all their hashes in a
> set and one pass over the text checks all of them. That's how plagiarism detection and content
> deduplication work — hash every k-length window and look for repeats. It also extends naturally to
> two-dimensional matching, which KMP doesn't.

---

### Z Algorithm

#### Kya hai

Ek string ke liye `Z` array banata hai jahan `Z[i]` = us position se shuru hone wala **sabse
lamba substring jo poori string ka prefix bhi ho**.
*Analogy:* har position par poochhna — "yahan se aage kitne characters bilkul shuruaat jaise
hain?"

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

Ek `[l, r]` window maintain hoti hai — abhi tak mila hua **sabse door tak jaane wala** prefix
match. Agar `i` us window ke andar hai, to `Z[i]` ka answer **pehle se compute ho chuki** mirror
position `Z[i-l]` se shuru mein hi mil jaata hai; sirf window ke bahar wala hissa manually
extend karna padta hai. Isliye total kaam linear rehta hai.

#### Code

```python
def z_array(s):
    """Z[i] = s[i:] aur s ka longest common prefix. Z[0] convention se len(s)."""
    n = len(s)                                      # 1
    z = [0] * n                                     # 2
    if n == 0:                                      # 3
        return z                                    # 4
    z[0] = n                                        # 5
    l = r = 0                                       # 6
    for i in range(1, n):                           # 7
        if i < r:                                   # 8
            z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l])             # 9
        while i + z[i] < n and s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]:   # 10
            z[i] += 1                               # 11
        if i + z[i] > r:                            # 12
            l, r = i, i + z[i]                      # 13
    return z                                        # 14


def z_search(text, pattern, sep="\x00"):
    """Pattern matching: pattern + separator + text ka Z array."""
    combined = pattern + sep + text                 # 15
    z = z_array(combined)                           # 16
    m = len(pattern)                                # 17
    return [i - m - 1 for i in range(m + 1, len(combined))
            if z[i] == m]                           # 18
```

**Line-by-line:**

5. `Z[0]` ko poori length maan lena convention hai (khud se match to poora hi hoga).
6. `[l, r)` = sabse right tak pahunchne wala known prefix-match ka interval.
8-9. **Ye line hi Z algorithm hai.** `i` window ke andar hai, to `s[i..r)` = `s[i-l..r-l)`
   already pata hai. `min` isliye kyunki mirror ka answer window se bahar nikal sakta hai —
   uske aage ka data hume abhi confirm nahi.
10-11. Bache hue characters manually match karo. **Ye loop kul milakar O(n) baar hi chalta hai**
   kyunki har successful comparison `r` ko aage badhata hai, aur `r` kabhi ghatta nahi.
12-13. Nayi window agar zyada door tak jaati hai to update.

15-18. **Concatenation trick.** Separator aisa chuno jo dono strings mein na ho, warna `Z[i]`
   `m` se bada ho sakta hai aur galat matches milenge. `z[i] == m` matlab poora pattern wahan
   se match hua; original index = `i - m - 1`.

#### Compact dry run — `s = "aabxaab"`

| i | i < r? | Initial z[i] | Extend | Final | [l, r) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nahi | 0 | a==a, b!=a | **1** | [1,2) |
| 2 | nahi | 0 | b!=a | **0** | [1,2) |
| 3 | nahi | 0 | x!=a | **0** | [1,2) |
| 4 | nahi | 0 | a,a,b match | **3** | [4,7) |
| 5 | haan (5<7) | min(2, z[1]=1) = 1 | b!=a par window | **1** | [4,7) |
| 6 | haan | min(1, z[2]=0) = 0 | b!=a | **0** | [4,7) |

`z = [7,1,0,0,3,1,0]`. Note `i=5` par hume **koi comparison nahi karni padi** — mirror se answer
mil gaya. Yahi speed ka source hai.

#### Complexity

| | Value | Kyun |
|---|---|---|
| Time | **O(n)** | Inner while ka har successful step `r` ko strictly aage badhata hai; `r` max `n` tak jaa sakta hai |
| Space | **O(n)** | Z array |
| Pattern search | **O(n + m)** | Combined string par ek pass |

#### Z vs KMP

| | Z | KMP |
|---|---|---|
| Kya deta hai | Har position par prefix-match ki length | Fallback table |
| Streaming text par | **Nahi** (poori string chahiye) | **Haan** (online) |
| Samajhne mein | Aasan (ek window) | Mushkil (recursive fallback) |
| Extra uses | Distinct substrings, string periodicity, compression | Automata, multiple-pattern base |

Interview mein agar KMP ka LPS yaad na aaye to **Z algorithm bol dena bilkul valid hai** — same
complexity, aur derive karna aasan hai.

> **Interview answer:** The Z array gives, for every position, the length of the longest substring
> starting there that is also a prefix of the whole string. It's computed in linear time by
> maintaining the rightmost window that is known to match the prefix — if the current index falls
> inside that window, its answer is available from the mirrored position and only the part beyond
> the window needs real comparisons.
>
> The linearity argument is that every successful character comparison pushes the right boundary
> forward, and that boundary never moves backwards, so the total comparison count is bounded by n.
>
> For pattern matching I concatenate pattern, a separator that appears in neither string, and the
> text, then every index where Z equals the pattern length is a match. That's O(n plus m), the same
> as KMP.
>
> I usually prefer Z in an interview because it's easier to derive under pressure than KMP's prefix
> function, and the two are interchangeable for search. KMP still wins when the text arrives as a
> stream, since Z needs the whole string up front.

### Manacher Algorithm

#### Kya hai

Ek string ke **saare palindromic substrings** ko O(n) mein dhoondh leta hai — khaas kar longest
palindromic substring.
*Analogy:* aaine ke saamne khade ho kar dono taraf barabar dekhna, aur pehle se dekhe hue
reflections ko dobara na dekhna.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

Pehle string ko transform karo — har character ke beech `#` daal do, jisse **even aur odd
lambaai ke palindromes ek jaise ho jaate hain** (poori transformed string mein sab odd ho jaate
hain). Phir Z algorithm jaisa hi window trick: sabse door tak jaane wale palindrome ka centre aur
right boundary yaad rakho, aur andar wale positions ke liye **mirror ka answer reuse** karo.

#### Code

```python
def manacher(s):
    """Longest palindromic substring, O(n)."""
    if not s:                                       # 1
        return ""                                   # 2
    t = "#" + "#".join(s) + "#"                     # 3
    n = len(t)                                      # 4
    p = [0] * n                                     # 5
    centre = right = 0                              # 6
    for i in range(n):                              # 7
        if i < right:                               # 8
            p[i] = min(right - i, p[2 * centre - i])   # 9
        while (i - p[i] - 1 >= 0 and i + p[i] + 1 < n
               and t[i - p[i] - 1] == t[i + p[i] + 1]):   # 10
            p[i] += 1                               # 11
        if i + p[i] > right:                        # 12
            centre, right = i, i + p[i]             # 13
    best = max(range(n), key=lambda k: p[k])        # 14
    start = (best - p[best]) // 2                   # 15
    return s[start:start + p[best]]                 # 16
```

**Line-by-line:**

3. **Transform.** `"aba"` → `"#a#b#a#"`. Ab har palindrome ka centre ek single index hai, chahe
   original mein wo character tha ya do characters ke beech ki jagah. **Ye ek line poori
   even/odd problem khatam kar deti hai.**
5. `p[i]` = `i` ke around palindrome ka radius (transformed string mein), jo original string
   mein us palindrome ki **exact length** ke barabar nikalta hai.
8-9. `2*centre - i` = `i` ka mirror. Mirror ka answer copy karo, par `right - i` se zyada nahi —
   uske aage ka data verified nahi hai.
10-11. Boundaries check karke expand.
12-13. Naya sabse door jaane wala palindrome mila to window update.
14-16. Sabse bada radius, aur transformed index se original index nikaalna: `(best - p[best]) // 2`.

#### Compact dry run — `s = "abaaba"` → `t = "#a#b#a#a#b#a#"` (n=13)

| i | t[i] | p[i] | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | a | 1 | `"a"` |
| 3 | b | 3 | `"aba"` |
| 6 | # | **6** | `"abaaba"` — poori string |
| 7 | a | 1 | mirror se |
| 9 | b | 3 | mirror se, bina extra work |

Max `p` = 6 at `i=6`. `start = (6-6)//2 = 0`, length 6 → `"abaaba"`.

#### Complexity

| | Value | Kyun |
|---|---|---|
| Time | **O(n)** | Wahi argument jaise Z — inner while ka har step `right` ko aage badhata hai |
| Space | **O(n)** | Transformed string + `p` array |
| Alternative (expand from centre) | **O(n²)** time, **O(1)** space | 2n-1 centres, har ek se O(n) expand |

**Sach ye hai:** interview mein **expand-from-centre** wala O(n²) solution aksar kaafi hota hai
aur likhna bohot aasan hai. Manacher tab likho jab explicitly O(n) maanga jaaye ya aap dikhana
chahte ho ki aapne mirror-reuse idea samjha hai. **DP solution (O(n²) time, O(n²) space) sabse
kharaab option hai** — same time, zyada space.

> **Interview answer:** Manacher finds the longest palindromic substring in linear time. Two ideas
> carry it. First, interleaving the string with separator characters makes every palindrome
> odd-length, which removes the even/odd case split entirely. Second, it maintains the rightmost
> palindrome found so far, and for any index inside it, the mirrored index's radius is a valid
> starting guess — capped by the distance to the boundary, since anything past that isn't verified
> yet.
>
> The linear bound comes from the same argument as the Z algorithm: every extra character
> comparison pushes the right boundary forward and it never retreats.
>
> In practice I'd usually offer expand-around-centre first: 2n-1 centres, expanding outward, O(n
> squared) time but O(1) space and about six lines. It's fast enough for typical constraints and
> much harder to get wrong. I'd write Manacher when linear time is explicitly required. What I'd
> avoid is the two-dimensional DP version — it's the same quadratic time as expand-around-centre
> but with quadratic space, so it's strictly worse.

### Practical String Operations for QA

#### Kya hai

Wo string kaam jo QA/SDET role mein **roz** aate hain — log parsing, response comparison,
normalisation, fuzzy matching — aur unka sahi complexity-aware tareeka.
*Analogy:* upar wale algorithms exam ke liye hain; ye section us toolbox ke liye hai jo aap
Monday subah kholte ho.

#### Kaise kaam karta hai

Do rules kaafi hain. **Ek:** Python strings **immutable** hain, isliye loop mein `+=` karna
O(n²) hai — hamesha `list` + `join`. **Do:** built-in operations C mein likhe hain, to `in`,
`str.find`, `re` aksar aapke hand-written KMP se tez chalenge.

#### Code

```python
import re
from collections import Counter


def build_log_line(fields):
    """GALAT vs SAHI concatenation."""
    slow = ""                                       # 1
    for f in fields:                                # 2
        slow += str(f) + " "                        # 3
    fast = " ".join(str(f) for f in fields)         # 4
    return slow.strip(), fast                       # 5


def normalise_response(text):
    """Compare karne se pehle noise hatao — flaky assertions ka ilaaj."""
    text = text.strip().lower()                     # 6
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text)                # 7
    text = re.sub(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T[\d:.]+Z?", "<TS>", text)   # 8
    text = re.sub(r"\b[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}"
                  r"-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}\b", "<UUID>", text)  # 9
    return text                                     # 10


def is_anagram(a, b):
    """O(n) — sorting O(n log n) se behtar."""
    return Counter(a) == Counter(b)                 # 11


def longest_unique_substring(s):
    """Sliding window, O(n). Duplicate-free longest run."""
    seen = {}                                       # 12
    best = start = 0                                # 13
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):                      # 14
        if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= start:        # 15
            start = seen[ch] + 1                    # 16
        seen[ch] = i                                # 17
        if i - start + 1 > best:                    # 18
            best = i - start + 1                    # 19
    return best                                     # 20


def parse_log_levels(lines):
    """Ek pass mein counts — regex compile ek hi baar."""
    pat = re.compile(r"^\S+\s+(\w+)\s")             # 21
    counts = Counter()                              # 22
    for line in lines:                              # 23
        m = pat.match(line)                         # 24
        if m:                                       # 25
            counts[m.group(1)] += 1                 # 26
    return counts                                   # 27
```

**Line-by-line:**

1-3. **Anti-pattern.** Har `+=` naya string banata hai aur poora content copy karta hai —
   `n` iterations mein O(n²) bytes copy. 10,000 log lines par ye naapne layak dhima hai.
4. `join` pehle total length calculate karta hai, ek baar allocate karta hai, phir copy — **O(n)**.
6-9. **Normalisation** — flaky test assertions ki sabse badi wajah timestamps aur UUIDs hote
   hain. Unhe placeholder se badal do, phir compare karo. Ye "80% of my flaky failures" wala fix
   hai.
7. `\s+ → " "` — HTML/JSON whitespace differences khatam.
11. `Counter` comparison O(n) hai; `sorted(a) == sorted(b)` O(n log n). Chhote strings par
   farak nahi, 1 MB payload par dikhta hai.
15-16. `seen[ch] >= start` — **`>= start` zaroori hai**, warna window ke bahar wale purane
   duplicates bhi window ko peeche kheench lenge. Ye sabse common sliding-window bug hai.
21. **`re.compile` loop ke bahar.** Andar rakhoge to Python har baar cache lookup karega — kaam
   karega par slow, aur intent bhi saaf nahi hota.

#### Compact complexity table — jo roz use hota hai

| Operation | Complexity | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `s1 + s2` | O(len(s1)+len(s2)) | Loop mein **kabhi nahi** |
| `"".join(parts)` | O(total) | Hamesha yahi |
| `sub in s` | O(n·m) worst, ~O(n) typical | CPython optimised, C speed |
| `s.replace(a, b)` | O(n) | Naya string banata hai |
| `s.split(d)` | O(n) | Saare pieces memory mein |
| `s[i]` | O(1) | |
| `s[i:j]` | **O(j-i)** | Loop mein slicing = chhupa hua O(n²) |
| `len(s)` | O(1) | Stored |
| `re.match` | O(n) se exponential | Catastrophic backtracking se bacho |
| `sorted(s)` | O(n log n) | |
| `Counter(s)` | O(n) | Anagram/frequency ke liye |

#### Ek regex warning — catastrophic backtracking

`(a+)+b` jaise nested quantifiers `"aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaX"` par exponential time le lete hain.
Ye real ReDoS vulnerability hai aur test suites ko hang karti hai. **Rule:** nested quantifiers
se bacho, aur possible ho to regex ki jagah `split`/`in`/`startswith` use karo.

#### Kab actual algorithm likhna padta hai

| Situation | Solution |
|---|---|
| Ek pattern, ek text | `in` ya `str.find` — bas |
| **Hazaar** patterns, ek text | Aho-Corasick (ya Rabin-Karp with hash set) |
| Fuzzy / "close enough" match | Edit distance ya `difflib.SequenceMatcher` |
| Do bade files ka diff | LCS-based — `difflib.unified_diff` |
| Streaming log par live match | KMP (online, buffer nahi chahiye) |
| Ek hi text par bohot saare queries | Suffix array / trie — preprocessing amortise ho jaati hai |

> **Interview answer:** For day-to-day string work I care about two things. First, Python strings
> are immutable, so building one with plus-equals in a loop is quadratic — I always collect pieces
> in a list and join once. The same trap hides in repeated slicing inside a loop, since each slice
> copies.
>
> Second, the built-ins are implemented in C, so the substring operator will usually beat a
> hand-written KMP for a single search. I only reach for a real algorithm when the shape of the
> problem demands it: many patterns against one text suggests Aho-Corasick or hashing, fuzzy
> matching suggests edit distance, and diffing two files is LCS, which is what difflib already
> gives me.
>
> The QA-specific piece is normalisation. Most flaky string assertions come from timestamps, UUIDs
> and whitespace differences, so I normalise those to placeholders before comparing rather than
> loosening the assertion. And I watch for catastrophic backtracking in regexes — nested quantifiers
> can turn a log parser into a hang on a single malformed line, which is a real denial-of-service
> class of bug, not just a performance issue.
